market_physics · econophysics feature library · documentation

Market Physics

A Python library of physics-inspired quantitative features for financial time series. Each of its 147 indicators borrows a measurement concept from a branch of physics — mechanics, gravitation, electromagnetism, thermodynamics, information theory, chaos, fractal geometry, random matrix theory — and applies it as a descriptive estimator over OHLCV market data.

16 families + energy 147 indicators v0.1.3 source 37730ca python 3.12+ pandas · numpy
Scope

Every output is a descriptive feature, not a trading signal. The library is not a buy/sell generator, not a strategy framework, and not a backtester. Physics names are analogies for the estimators — the library makes no claim that markets obey physical law, only that physical measurement concepts produce useful descriptive coordinates for market state.

Why econophysics features

Standard technical features describe price with price's own vocabulary: averages of it, ranges of it, ratios of it. Physics offers an alternative: a century of instruments built to measure any dynamical system — how disordered it is (entropy), how much energy a motion carries (mechanics), how strongly components couple (networks), whether fluctuations are self-similar (fractals), how far from equilibrium the system sits (thermodynamics). Applied to a return series, these instruments are meant to measure different axes of market state than the classical vocabulary, which is what makes them candidate inputs to research pipelines. The library does not claim they are uncorrelated with classical indicators — several reduce to familiar statistics once the physics name is set aside (market_velocity is the close-to-close return, damping_ratio a short-over-long volatility ratio) — and where two of its own indicators compute the same quantity under different names, the metadata says so under known_relationship.

Each family chapter below opens with the physics — the original phenomenon, the governing relations, and how the estimator transplants them to market data — then documents every indicator: signature, physical picture, parameters, return contract, and the indicator computed on a shared reference dataset.

One contract, every indicator

Indicators take a pandas OHLCV dataframe (columns open, high, low, close, volume — each function validates only the columns it actually reads) plus parameters, and return an IndicatorResult:

from market_physics.dynamics import market_velocity

result = market_velocity(df)
result.name                       # "market_velocity"
result.values                     # pd.Series aligned to df.index, NaN during warm-up
result.metadata["return_method"]   # "pct" — every parameter used rides along
result.metadata["formula"]         # "returns"
result.metadata["limitation"]      # what the number is not
fieldtypewhat it holds
namestrIndicator identifier
valuespd.SeriesComputed series, index-aligned to the input; NaN during the warm-up window
metadatadict[str, Any]The parameters used (normalize is recorded as normalized, a column choice through source_columns), plus descriptive keys (below)

IndicatorResult is a slotted dataclass that type-checks its three fields when it is built. The metadata vocabulary is shared across families; counted over all 146 functions that return an IndicatorResult, called at their default parameters, the descriptive keys are:

keycarried bywhat it holds
methodall 146The estimator's identifier, e.g. "market_velocity" or "inverse_square_volume_profile"
interpretationall 146A plain-language reading of high and low values
limitationall 146What the number is not: estimator bias, parameter sensitivity, guards, and usually the statement that it is not a signal or prediction
source_columns144 — all but mutual_information and transfer_entropyThe input columns the call actually read; it follows the parameters (e.g. volume only when an option needs it)
formula136 — the ten multi-component composites list components insteadThe computation as a string, matching the parameters used
normalized69Whether a normalisation option was applied
expected_range67The stated output range as text — "0..1", "-1..1", "[-180, 180]", "non-negative", "approximately 0..1" …; often only under normalisation, and not on every bounded output (spectral_entropy and tail_pressure carry none)
known_relationship30Which other indicator computes the same or a closely related quantity
components, min_valid_components, warmup_note24 / 18 / 13For composites: the parts that are combined, how many must be defined before a bar is scored, and how that shapes the warm-up
bounded17An explicit True/False where boundedness needed stating (e.g. damping_ratio is unbounded)

One exception to the return type — gravity_levels returns a plain DataFrame of detected levels (one row per level, with rank, price, mass, strength, mass_share, side, distance_pct, zone_width_pct) rather than a time series; see its entry.

Two other input shapes — mutual_information(x, y) and transfer_entropy(source, target) take two pd.Series instead of a frame, and the networks family takes a wide multi-asset panel — one numeric column per asset, read as returns by default or as prices with input_type="prices" — instead of an OHLCV frame.

Conventions & errors

  • Warm-up — a rolling indicator with window w is NaN until enough observations exist; output stays aligned to the input index. Nested constructions extend it: a rolling statistic of returns starts a bar late (the first return is undefined), and a rolling mean of a rolling statistic roughly doubles the wait — free_energy_proxy at its default window=100 first emits at row 297 (zero-based). Composites with a min_valid_components parameter can emit before every component is ready. Passing the row check guarantees no exception, not a defined value: the entropy estimators accept a frame of exactly w rows but need w + 1 for their first value.
  • Undefined is NaN, not zero — a zero denominator, a window with no usable volume profile, or a volatility too small to tell apart from floating-point drift reads NaN rather than a balanced-looking 0.0 (one documented exception: normalised mutual_information reads 0.0 when either marginal entropy is zero). Since 0.1.1–0.1.2, every rolling standard deviation or variance that feeds a guard, ratio or aggregation is snapped to exact 0.0 on exactly-constant windows, so a full-history pass and a shorter tail pass over the same bars agree on flat data; the per-window estimators (entropy, Fourier, fractal, gravity profiles) were offset-invariant by construction.
  • Returns — functions with a return_method parameter accept "pct" (percentage change) or "log" (log returns, non-positive prices masked to NaN first). The default is family-specific: "pct" in dynamics, waves, statistical and energy; "log" in every other family that has the parameter. The twelve single-series entropy estimators have no return_method and always use percentage changes — of close, or of volume for the volume variants; mutual_information and transfer_entropy use the two series they are given as they are.
  • Windows are bars — every window, lookback, period and lag is measured in bars/candles of whatever timeframe you feed in, never clock time.
  • Validation — missing columns raise MissingColumnError; too few rows raise InsufficientDataError (both subclass MarketPhysicsError from market_physics.exceptions, also importable from the package root, so one except clause catches both); out-of-range parameters raise the built-in ValueError, and an input that is not a DataFrame the built-in TypeError — neither is a MarketPhysicsError subclass. The two-series entropy functions validate only their parameters; the networks family also raises ValueError for a non-numeric asset column.
  • Histogram bins — histogram-based indicators (the Shannon, Rényi and Tsallis entropies, mutual_information, transfer_entropy, return_distribution_pressure, and the four thermodynamics members with an entropy term) accept bins as "fd" (Freedman–Diaconis, default), "sqrt", "sturges", or an integer ≥ 2; a boolean is rejected. transfer_entropy defaults to bins=3 to keep its three-way joint table from going sparse. The gravity volume profiles use their own integer price_bins (≥ 2; 50 by default, 80 for gravity_levels). Normalised Shannon, Rényi and Tsallis entropies divide by a sample-size basis; the thermodynamics entropy terms divide by the number of occupied bins.

The reference dataset

Every chart in this documentation shows the indicator computed on the same synthetic OHLCV series: 1200 bars through four engineered regimes — a low-volatility uptrend (bars 0–400), sideways chop (400–700), a high-volatility crash with a volume surge (700–850, shaded red), and a decaying-volatility recovery (850–1200). The networks family runs on a companion 8-asset returns panel driven by the same market factor, with cross-asset correlation engineered per regime: 0.30 in the uptrend, 0.25 in the chop, 0.80 in the crash, 0.45 in the recovery (realised on this draw: 0.30 / 0.26 / 0.80 / 0.47) — so the many-body indicators face a textbook correlation spike. Synthetic data is used deliberately: because the regimes are known by construction, you can verify that each indicator responds the way its physics says it should. It is not market data.

Provenance — the series is regenerated deterministically (numpy seed 20260875, shocks de-meaned within each regime so every regime realises its designed drift) by the documentation generator; the 2026-07 generator was not preserved, so the curve differs in detail from the earlier page while keeping its regimes and correlations.

dynamics

Newtonian kinematics — velocity, force, work · 10 indicators

Classical mechanics begins with a single mapping: a body has a position x(t), and everything else — velocity, acceleration, momentum, force — is derived from how that position changes. The dynamics family makes the same move for markets: price is position. Once x(t) = P(t), the whole kinematic chain follows by differentiation:

v(t) = dx/dt  →  return of the close price
a(t) = dv/dt  →  change in the return
p(t) = m·v(t)  →  relative volume × return (volume plays mass)
F(t) = m·a(t)  →  relative volume × change in return
— m = volume ÷ its rolling mean over window (20 bars by default for momentum and force)

The interesting physics is in the role of mass. In mechanics, mass is the body's resistance to acceleration; here volume is the mass of a move, measured against its own rolling mean, so a bar traded on twice its recent average volume carries mass 2. A 2% move on heavy volume carries more momentum — in the literal p = mv sense — than the same move on thin volume, and by Newton's second law it takes a proportionally larger force to reverse it. This is why the family distinguishes velocity (how fast price moves) from momentum and force (how much participation is behind the motion).

Beyond the kinematic chain, the family borrows from oscillator theory and energetics. A damped oscillator loses amplitude at a rate set by its damping ratio; here the ratio compares short-horizon return amplitude with a longer one (standard deviation over 20 bars against 100 by default), so a value below 1 reads as recent oscillation damped and above 1 as amplified. Friction is motion lost to resistance: the share of the return path that cancels out instead of becoming net displacement, bounded in [0, 1]. Inertia is the tendency of a trend to persist, read as how consistently the sign of the return holds over the window — volume-weighted by default, so it can exceed 1. Work (W = F·d) is what volume expends pushing price over a distance: relative volume times return, summed over the window. An impulse is a large force delivered over a short interval — a move that is large relative to its own recent volatility, scaled by participation. And potential energy accumulates when price is displaced from its equilibrium, here the squared distance of the close from a rolling VWAP (or SMA), divided by that level squared by default — a compressed-spring picture the library explicitly does not read as a mean-reversion signal.

Some members are the same arithmetic as other indicators, and their metadata says so: market_momentum at scale=1 equals work_done_by_volume(cumulative=False), damping_ratio equals turbulence's volatility_cascade in ratio mode, and market_friction equals turbulence's unweighted market_viscosity. The equalities hold at matched parameters, and the family's return_method default is "pct" where turbulence defaults to "log".

When to reach for this family: trend diagnosis. It answers, in a common mechanical vocabulary, how fast the market is moving, whether the motion is speeding up or decaying, and how much mass is behind it.

damping_ratio

from market_physics.dynamics import damping_ratio

damping_ratio(
    df: pd.DataFrame,
    window: int = 100,
    *,
    short_window: int = 20,
    return_method: Literal['pct', 'log'] = 'pct',
) -> IndicatorResult

Damping Ratio borrows the language of damped oscillators, where damping describes how quickly oscillation amplitude decays relative to a reference. Mapping price to position, it compares the short-horizon amplitude of returns against the long-horizon amplitude:

  • short_amp -> rolling standard deviation of returns over short_window,
  • long_amp -> rolling standard deviation of returns over window,
  • ratio -> short_amp / long_amp.

Values below 1 describe short-term amplitude that is small relative to the longer horizon (recent oscillation is damped); values above 1 describe short-term amplitude that exceeds the longer horizon (recent oscillation is amplified). This is a descriptive amplitude ratio only — it is not a trading signal and carries no directional recommendation.

Equivalent to turbulence.volatility_cascade(mode='ratio') at matched parameters; exposed here as a classical-mechanics damping/amplification ratio.

core quantity std(returns, short_window) / std(returns, window)

Parameters
nametypedefaultdescription
dfpd.DataFrame—OHLCV dataframe. Only the close column is required.
windowint100Long-horizon rolling window for the reference amplitude (>= 2, and strictly greater than short_window).
short_window kw-onlyint20Short-horizon rolling window for the recent amplitude (>= 2 and less than window).
return_method kw-onlyLiteral['pct', 'log']'pct'How to compute returns. "pct" uses percentage change; "log" uses log returns.
Returns

An IndicatorResult aligned to df index, with NaN during the warm-up period and wherever the result is undefined (e.g. zero long-horizon amplitude).

Raises
ValueErrorIf window or short_window is less than 2, short_window is not less than window, or return_method is invalid.
MissingColumnErrorIf the close column is missing.
InsufficientDataErrorIf df has fewer than window + 1 rows.
Example
# df: OHLCV dataframe (open, high, low, close, volume)
from market_physics.dynamics import damping_ratio

result = damping_ratio(df)
result.name                        # "damping_ratio"
result.metadata["formula"]         # "std(returns, short_window) / std(returns, window)"
result.values.iloc[-1]             # 1.00586 on the synthetic dataset
result.values.first_valid_index()  # 100 — NaN during warm-up

Reading it — Descriptive amplitude ratio: values below 1 describe short-term amplitude that is small relative to the longer horizon (recent oscillation damped) and values above 1 describe short-term amplitude that exceeds it (recent oscillation amplified). Descriptive only — not a signal.

Related — Equivalent to turbulence.volatility_cascade(mode='ratio') at matched parameters; exposed here as a classical-mechanics damping/amplification ratio.

Limitation — Descriptive amplitude-ratio analogy; a non-negative, unbounded ratio (not in [0, 1]). The long-horizon volatility denominator is float-drift-guarded (masked to NaN on near-constant returns). Not physical mechanics, not a prediction, and not a trading signal.

impulse_energy

from market_physics.dynamics import impulse_energy

impulse_energy(
    df: pd.DataFrame,
    window: int = 50,
    *,
    return_method: Literal['pct', 'log'] = 'pct',
    scale: float = 1.0,
) -> IndicatorResult

Impulse Energy borrows the mechanics idea of an impulse — a large force delivered over a short interval that produces a sudden change in motion. Mapping price to position, it measures how sharp a move is relative to its own recent volatility and scales that shock by the participating mass:

  • shock -> abs(returns) / rolling_std(returns) (move size in units of its own recent volatility),
  • mass -> normalised volume (current volume relative to its rolling mean),
  • impulse -> shock * mass * scale.

Impulse Energy is unsigned: a sharp up-move and an equally sharp down-move of the same standardised magnitude and volume produce the same impulse. Higher values describe sudden, volume-backed shocks; values near zero describe calm, low-participation movement. This is a descriptive feature only — it is not a trading signal and carries no directional recommendation.

core quantity (abs(returns) / rolling_std(returns, window)) * normalized_volume * scale

Parameters
nametypedefaultdescription
dfpd.DataFrame—OHLCV dataframe. Requires the close and volume columns.
windowint50Lookback window for the rolling volatility and rolling volume mean (>= 2).
return_method kw-onlyLiteral['pct', 'log']'pct'How to compute returns. "pct" uses percentage change; "log" uses log returns.
scale kw-onlyfloat1.0Positive multiplier applied to the final series for easier visualisation. Does not alter the relative shape of the values.
Returns

An IndicatorResult aligned to df index, with NaN during the warm-up period and wherever the result is undefined (e.g. zero rolling volatility or zero rolling volume mean).

Raises
ValueErrorIf window is less than 2, scale is not greater than 0, or return_method is invalid.
MissingColumnErrorIf close or volume is missing.
InsufficientDataErrorIf df has fewer than window + 1 rows.
Example
# df: OHLCV dataframe (open, high, low, close, volume)
from market_physics.dynamics import impulse_energy

result = impulse_energy(df)
result.name                        # "impulse_energy"
result.metadata["formula"]         # "(abs(returns) / rolling_std(returns, window)) * normalized_volume * scale"
result.values.iloc[-1]             # 0.804819 on the synthetic dataset
result.values.first_valid_index()  # 50 — NaN during warm-up

Reading it — Unsigned descriptive impulse: higher values describe sudden, volume-backed shocks (a move that is large relative to its own recent volatility, backed by above-average participation) and values near zero describe calm, low-participation movement. Descriptive only — not a signal.

Limitation — Descriptive mechanics analogy (standardized shock times participation); unbounded and heavy-tailed. The volatility denominator is float-drift-guarded (masked to NaN on near-constant returns). Not physical mechanics, not a prediction, and not a trading signal.

market_acceleration

from market_physics.dynamics import market_acceleration

market_acceleration(
    df: pd.DataFrame,
    window: int = 1,
    *,
    return_method: Literal['pct', 'log'] = 'pct',
    smooth: bool = False,
) -> IndicatorResult

Market Acceleration is the classical-mechanics analogue of acceleration — the rate of change of velocity. Mapping price to position, velocity is the close-price return and acceleration is the change in that return from one bar to the next.

Positive acceleration describes velocity increasing (price motion speeding up in the positive direction or decelerating downward); negative describes the opposite. This is a descriptive second-order rate of change only — it is not a trading signal and carries no directional recommendation.

core quantity diff(returns)

return_method kw-onlyLiteral['pct', 'log']'pct'How to compute returns. "pct" uses percentage change; "log" uses log returns.
smooth kw-onlyboolFalseIf True, average the acceleration over window observations.
Returns

An IndicatorResult aligned to df index, with NaN during the warm-up period.

Raises
ValueErrorIf window is less than 1 or return_method is invalid.
MissingColumnErrorIf the close column is missing.
InsufficientDataErrorIf df has fewer rows than needed for one defined output (3 when not smoothing, window + 2 when smoothing).
Example
# df: OHLCV dataframe (open, high, low, close, volume)
from market_physics.dynamics import market_acceleration

result = market_acceleration(df)
result.name                        # "market_acceleration"
result.metadata["formula"]         # "diff(returns)"
result.values.iloc[-1]             # 0.00136515 on the synthetic dataset
result.values.first_valid_index()  # 2 — NaN during warm-up

Reading it — Positive acceleration describes velocity increasing and negative describes velocity decreasing; the magnitude describes how quickly velocity is changing. Descriptive only — not a signal.

Window note — window only affects the output when smooth=True; otherwise it is retained for API consistency and validation.

Limitation — Descriptive second-order rate-of-change analogy (the return difference); signed and unbounded. Not physical acceleration, not a prediction, and not a trading signal.

market_force

from market_physics.dynamics import market_force

market_force(
    df: pd.DataFrame,
    window: int = 20,
    *,
    return_method: Literal['pct', 'log'] = 'pct',
    scale: float = 1.0,
) -> IndicatorResult

Market Force is the classical-mechanics analogue of Newton's second law F = m * a — mass times acceleration. Market mapping:

  • a (acceleration) -> change in close-price return (the first difference of velocity),
  • m (mass) -> normalised volume (current volume relative to its rolling mean),
  • F (force) -> normalized_volume * acceleration * scale.

Force is signed: positive values describe volume-backed acceleration in the positive direction and negative values describe the opposite. It is a descriptive feature only — not a trading signal and not a directional recommendation.

core quantity normalized_volume * diff(returns) * scale

Returns

An IndicatorResult aligned to df index, with NaN during the warm-up period and wherever the result is undefined (e.g. zero rolling volume mean).

Raises

Limitation — Descriptive mechanics analogy (signed m*a); unbounded and scaled by the arbitrary scale factor. Not physical force, not a prediction, and not a trading signal.

market_friction

from market_physics.dynamics import market_friction

market_friction(
    df: pd.DataFrame,
    window: int = 50,
    *,
    return_method: Literal['pct', 'log'] = 'pct',
) -> IndicatorResult

Market Friction borrows the idea of a path that dissipates energy through resistance. Mapping price to position, it compares the total distance travelled by the return path against the net displacement over the same window:

  • path_length -> sum of absolute returns (total ground covered),
  • net_displacement -> absolute sum of returns (straight-line progress),
  • friction -> 1 - net_displacement / path_length.

The value lives in [0, 1]. Near 0 describes efficient, directional movement (the path is nearly a straight line and almost all motion translates into net displacement). Near 1 describes noisy movement with little net displacement (the path wanders and cancels out, like motion lost to friction).

This is a descriptive feature only — it is not a trading signal and carries no directional recommendation.

Equivalent to turbulence.market_viscosity(volume_weighted=False) at matched parameters; related to returns-path roughness / geodesic-dissipation style measures.

core quantity 1 - abs(sum(returns, window)) / sum(abs(returns), window)

Parameters
nametypedefaultdescription
dfpd.DataFrame—OHLCV dataframe. Only the close column is required.
windowint50Rolling window over which the path is measured (>= 2).
return_method kw-onlyLiteral['pct', 'log']'pct'How to compute returns. "pct" uses percentage change; "log" uses log returns.
Returns

An IndicatorResult aligned to df index, with NaN during the warm-up period and wherever the result is undefined (e.g. zero path length over a flat window).

Raises
ValueErrorIf window is less than 2 or return_method is invalid.
MissingColumnErrorIf the close column is missing.

Example
# df: OHLCV dataframe (open, high, low, close, volume)
from market_physics.dynamics import market_friction

result = market_friction(df)
result.name                        # "market_friction"
result.metadata["formula"]         # "1 - abs(sum(returns, window)) / sum(abs(returns), window)"
result.values.iloc[-1]             # 0.841244 on the synthetic dataset
result.values.first_valid_index()  # 50 — NaN during warm-up

Reading it — Descriptive path-efficiency measure in [0, 1]: near 0 describes efficient, directional movement (net displacement close to the path length) and near 1 describes noisy movement with little net displacement. Descriptive only — not a signal.

Related — Equivalent to turbulence.market_viscosity(volume_weighted=False) at matched parameters; related to returns-path roughness / geodesic-dissipation style measures.

Limitation — Descriptive path-efficiency analogy bounded in [0, 1]; NaN over a flat (zero path length) window. Not physical friction, not a prediction, and not a trading signal.

market_momentum

from market_physics.dynamics import market_momentum

market_momentum(
    df: pd.DataFrame,
    window: int = 20,
    *,
    return_method: Literal['pct', 'log'] = 'pct',
    scale: float = 1.0,
) -> IndicatorResult

Market Momentum is the classical-mechanics analogue of momentum p = m * v — mass times velocity. Market mapping:

  • v (velocity) -> close-price return,
  • m (mass) -> normalised volume (current volume relative to its rolling mean),
  • p (momentum) -> normalized_volume * return * scale.

Unlike market_physics.energy.momentum_energy (which squares the return and is therefore unsigned), this momentum is signed: positive values describe volume-backed upward motion and negative values describe volume-backed downward motion. It is a descriptive feature only — not the same quantity as momentum energy, and not a trading signal.

At matched parameters with scale=1, equals work_done_by_volume(cumulative=False); momentum is exposed as the signed m * v framing.

market_potential_energy

from market_physics.dynamics import market_potential_energy

market_potential_energy(
    df: pd.DataFrame,
    window: int = 100,
    *,
    equilibrium: Literal['vwap', 'sma'] = 'vwap',
    normalize: bool = True,
) -> IndicatorResult

Market Potential Energy borrows the idea of the potential energy stored in a displacement from equilibrium (as in a spring, U = 0.5 * k * x^2). Mapping price to position, the equilibrium is a rolling centre of price and the displacement is how far the current close sits from that centre:

  • center -> a rolling equilibrium price ("sma" rolling mean or "vwap" volume-weighted average price),
  • displacement -> close - center,
  • potential -> displacement ** 2 (optionally divided by center ** 2 when normalize).

Market Potential Energy is unsigned: it grows with the squared distance from equilibrium regardless of which side of the centre price sits on. It describes how stretched price is relative to its rolling centre; it is explicitly not a mean-reversion signal and implies no expectation that price will return to the centre. This is a descriptive feature only — it is not a trading signal and carries no directional recommendation.

Closely related to gravity.field_potential(center='center_of_mass') at matched parameters; market_potential_energy uses a rolling VWAP-style equilibrium, while field_potential uses a binned volume-profile center.

core quantity (close - center) ** 2 / center ** 2

Parameters

dfpd.DataFrame—OHLCV dataframe. Requires close; also requires volume when equilibrium is "vwap".
windowint100Lookback window for the rolling equilibrium (>= 2).
equilibrium kw-onlyLiteral['vwap', 'sma']'vwap'Which rolling centre to use. "sma" uses the rolling mean of close; "vwap" uses the rolling volume-weighted average price.
normalize kw-onlyboolTrueIf True, divide the squared displacement by center ** 2 to produce a scale-free measure.
Returns

An IndicatorResult aligned to df index, with NaN during the warm-up period and wherever the result is undefined (e.g. zero rolling volume for "vwap" or a zero centre when normalising).

Raises
ValueErrorIf window is less than 2 or equilibrium is not one of "vwap" or "sma".
MissingColumnErrorIf a required column is missing (close, plus volume when equilibrium is "vwap").
InsufficientDataErrorIf df has fewer than window rows.
Example

from market_physics.dynamics import market_potential_energy

result = market_potential_energy(df)
result.name                        # "market_potential_energy"

result.values.first_valid_index()  # 99 — NaN during warm-up

Reading it — Unsigned descriptive measure of how far price is displaced from its rolling equilibrium centre: larger values describe price that is more stretched from the centre, regardless of side. Not a mean-reversion signal — it implies no expectation that price will return to the centre. Descriptive only — not a signal.

Related — Closely related to gravity.field_potential(center='center_of_mass') at matched parameters; market_potential_energy uses a rolling VWAP-style equilibrium, while field_potential uses a binned volume-profile center.

Limitation — Descriptive displacement-energy analogy; non-negative and unbounded (the normalised form is scale-free but not necessarily bounded). Explicitly not a mean-reversion signal, not physical potential energy, not a prediction, and not a trading signal.

from market_physics.dynamics import trend_inertia

trend_inertia(
    df: pd.DataFrame,
    window: int = 50,
    *,
    return_method: Literal['pct', 'log'] = 'pct',
    volume_weighted: bool = True,
) -> IndicatorResult

Trend Inertia borrows the classical-mechanics idea of inertia — a body's tendency to keep moving in the same direction. Mapping price to position, the return direction plays the role of the direction of motion; inertia measures how consistently that direction persists over the window.

When volume_weighted is False the value lives roughly in [0, 1]: high inertia describes a persistent directional regime (the return direction rarely flips), low inertia describes choppy, unstable direction (the sign flips often and cancels out). When volume_weighted is True, each direction is scaled by normalised volume so that high-participation bars contribute more to the persistence measure. Normalised volume acts as a mass/amplifier, so weighted values may exceed 1.0 when persistent direction coincides with above-average volume; weighted values are intentionally left unclipped so the amplification is preserved.

This is a descriptive feature only — it is not a trading signal and carries no directional recommendation.

core quantity abs(rolling_mean(sign(returns) * normalized_volume, window))

volume_weighted kw-onlyboolTrueIf True, weight each direction by normalised volume.
Returns

from market_physics.dynamics import work_done_by_volume

work_done_by_volume(
    df: pd.DataFrame,
    window: int = 50,
    *,
    return_method: Literal['pct', 'log'] = 'pct',
    cumulative: bool = True,
) -> IndicatorResult

Work Done by Volume borrows the mechanics definition of work — force applied over a displacement (W = F * d). Mapping price to position, the displacement is the return and the force is proxied by the participating mass (normalised volume):

  • mass -> normalised volume (current volume relative to its rolling mean),
  • work_step -> mass * returns (signed per-bar work),
  • work -> the per-bar work, or its rolling sum when cumulative.

Work is signed: positive values describe volume-backed work in the positive direction and negative values describe volume-backed work in the negative direction; the rolling sum accumulates and can partially cancel. This is a descriptive feature only — it is not a trading signal and carries no directional recommendation.

When cumulative=False and parameters are matched, equals market_momentum(scale=1); cumulative=True is the rolling sum of the same work/momentum step.

gravity

Gravitation — mass, potential wells, orbits · 7 indicators

Newtonian gravity says mass curves the space around it: a body of mass M creates a potential U(r) = −GM/r, and objects roll downhill toward it. The gravity family transplants this to the price axis. Traded volume at a price level is mass: a level where a large amount of volume changed hands is a massive body sitting on the price line, and in the analogy it pulls on price the way a planet pulls on a satellite.

F(P)  =  Σi sign(Li − P) · G·mi / ((Li − P)² + s)   — net pull on the latest close P; mi volume mass in the price bin centred at Li
U(P)  =  (P − L̄)² / P²   — field potential about the volume-mass centre L̄
— softening s = max(ε, bin width²); with normalize=True F is divided by Σ|force|, so it lies in [−1, 1] and G cancels

The intuition behind the analogy is behavioural: at a heavily-traded level, many positions were opened. Those positions are memory — resting orders, break-even stops, anchored expectations — and traders expect them to pull price back when it wanders. The library encodes the geometry of that picture, not the expectation: every gravity time series is documented as not a support/resistance prediction, and the force and distance readings also as not a mean-reversion claim. The family builds the picture in two steps. First, a volume profile: over a rolling lookback (200 bars by default) traded volume is histogrammed into 50 price bins, either at each candle's close (price_source="close") or spread evenly across every bin its low–high range overlaps ("range"); zero, negative or missing volume contributes no mass. Second, readings of that profile against the latest close: the net inverse-square pull on it (gravity_wells) and that pull's bar-to-bar change (field_gradient); the split of mass above versus below it (gravitational_balance); how concentrated the mass is, as a Herfindahl index rescaled so a uniform profile reads 0 and a single bin 1 (mass_concentration_score); and how far price sits from the highest-mass bin or the centre of mass — signed and relative to the close as orbital_deviation, squared as field_potential.

gravity_levels is the static counterpart. It builds one profile over the last 500 bars (80 bins), takes the strongest bins as candidates, merges candidates that sit within 0.5% of each other into zones, and returns at most eight of them, each labelled support, resistance or current relative to the latest close. gravity_wells and field_gradient default to the close profile; the other five default to the range profile.

Readers who know market-profile analysis will recognise high-volume nodes; the gravity framing adds the field formalism — a net force, a centre of mass, a potential about it — so the distance to a level and the mass behind it combine into one number. At default settings a window whose profile is unusable (no volume, or a flat price range) reads NaN, never a balanced-looking zero.

When to reach for this family: support/resistance in continuous form. Instead of binary "level broken / level held", you get continuous readings of where traded volume sits and where price is within it.

field_gradientfield_potentialgravitational_balancegravity_levelsgravity_wellsmass_concentration_scoreorbital_deviation

field_gradient

from market_physics.gravity import field_gradient

field_gradient(
    df: pd.DataFrame,
    lookback: int = 200,
    *,
    price_bins: int = 50,
    gravity_constant: float = 1.0,
    epsilon: float = 1e-09,
    normalize: bool = True,
    price_source: Literal['close', 'range'] = 'close',
) -> IndicatorResult

Physical analogy

The Field Gradient is the bar-to-bar change in the net gravitational field that market_physics.gravity.gravity_wells.gravity_wells computes. Where that field describes the current net pull on price, its gradient describes how that pull is changing:

field    = net signed inverse-square field of the rolling volume profile
gradient = field.diff()

The net field is produced by the shared market_physics.gravity._field helper — the same calculation gravity_wells uses — so the two stay consistent. Because the gradient is a first difference, its first defined value requires two consecutive field values; the warm-up therefore extends one bar beyond the field's own warm-up.

This indicator is descriptive only: it expresses the rate of change of a field value, not a buy/sell signal.

Interpretation:

  • positive gradient -> the field is becoming more positive (upward-pull- dominant relative to the previous bar),
  • negative gradient -> the field is becoming more negative (downward-pull- dominant relative to the previous bar),
  • near zero -> the field is relatively stable.

core quantity diff(net_gravitational_field)

gravity_constant kw-onlyfloat1.0Gravitational constant G scaling every force.
epsilon kw-onlyfloat1e-09Lower bound for the softening term added to distance^2.
normalize kw-onlyboolTrueIf True, normalise the underlying field before differencing.
price_source kw-onlyLiteral['close', 'range']'close'"close" assigns each candle's volume to its close bin; "range" distributes it across the bins overlapping the candle's low-high range.

from market_physics.gravity import field_potential

field_potential(
    df: pd.DataFrame,
    lookback: int = 200,
    *,
    price_bins: int = 50,
    price_source: Literal['close', 'range'] = 'range',
    normalize: bool = True,

) -> IndicatorResult

Physical analogy

In a gravitational (or spring) field, the potential energy of a body grows with the square of its displacement from equilibrium. Mapping that onto markets, the equilibrium is the volume-mass center of a rolling window and the displacement is how far the current price sits from it:

displacement = current_close - center_price
potential    = displacement ** 2

optionally divided by current_close ** 2 to give a simple, scale-free relative measure. The mass center is either the mass-weighted average of bin centers (center="center_of_mass") or the center of the highest-mass bin (center="dominant").

For each rolling lookback window a volume profile is built over price_bins price levels (see price_source).

This indicator is descriptive only. It measures how far price sits from a recent volume-mass equilibrium; it makes no mean-reversion claim and implies no expectation that price will move back toward the center.

Closely related to dynamics.market_potential_energy(equilibrium='vwap') at matched parameters; field_potential uses a binned volume-profile center and current-close normalization, while market_potential_energy uses the rolling VWAP-style equilibrium.

Interpretation:

  • higher -> price is farther from the recent volume-mass equilibrium,
  • lower -> price is closer to the recent volume-mass equilibrium.

core quantity (current_close - center_price) ** 2 / current_close ** 2

from market_physics.gravity import gravitational_balance

gravitational_balance(
    df: pd.DataFrame,
    lookback: int = 200,
    *,
    price_bins: int = 50,
    price_source: Literal['close', 'range'] = 'range',
    normalize: bool = True,
) -> IndicatorResult

Physical analogy

If high-volume price zones act like masses, then the current price sits inside a field whose mass is distributed above and below it. Gravitational Balance measures how that mass is split relative to the current price:

balance = mass_above - mass_below

optionally normalised by the total profile mass so the value lands roughly in [-1, 1].

For each rolling lookback window a volume profile is built over price_bins price levels (see price_source). Each bin is classified as above or below the current (latest close) price by comparing the bin's center to the current price; a bin whose center coincides exactly with the current price (a measure-zero, rare case) is treated neutrally and excluded from both sides. Because |mass_above - mass_below| never exceeds the total mass, the normalised value stays within [-1, 1].

This indicator is descriptive only: it summarises where volume mass sits relative to price, not a buy/sell signal.

Interpretation:

  • positive value -> more volume mass above the current price,
  • negative value -> more volume mass below the current price,
  • near zero -> upper and lower mass are balanced.

from market_physics.gravity import gravity_levels

gravity_levels(

Gravity Levels detects high-volume price zones that behave like gravitational mass concentrations. It builds a volume profile over a rolling lookback window — inspired by the idea that price levels where significant volume has traded act as "mass" — and surfaces the strongest discrete zones.

Unlike the time-series indicators in this package, gravity_levels returns a pandas.DataFrame: levels are discrete price zones, not a value per timestamp.

This is a descriptive level-detection utility, not a buy/sell signal, strategy, or backtest.

gravity_wells

from market_physics.gravity import gravity_wells

gravity_wells(
    df: pd.DataFrame,
    lookback: int = 200,
    *,
    price_bins: int = 50,
    gravity_constant: float = 1.0,
    epsilon: float = 1e-09,
    normalize: bool = True,
    price_source: Literal['close', 'range'] = 'close',
) -> IndicatorResult

Physical analogy

A gravity well is a region of space where mass concentrates and pulls nearby bodies toward it. Mapping that onto markets:

  • Price levels where significant volume has traded act as "masses".
  • The current price is the "body" experiencing attraction toward those high-mass price levels (think volume-profile points of control).
  • Closer high-volume zones exert a stronger pull, following an inverse-square style relationship.

For each rolling lookback window a volume profile is built over price_bins price levels. Each bin contributes a signed force toward the current (latest close) price:

signed_force = sign(distance) * G * mass / (distance^2 + softening)

where distance = bin_center - current_price and softening is max(epsilon, bin_width^2). The net field is the sum of those signed forces, optionally normalised by the total absolute force.

Volume profile sources (price_source):

  • "close" - each candle's volume is assigned to the bin its close falls in (point-of-trade approximation).
  • "range" - each candle's volume is distributed equally across every bin overlapping its low-high range (range-of-trade approximation).

This indicator is descriptive only: it expresses a gravitational field value, not a buy/sell signal.

Interpretation:

  • positive value -> stronger pull toward higher price zones,
  • negative value -> stronger pull toward lower price zones,
  • near zero -> balanced gravitational field.

core quantity signed_force = sign(distance) * G * mass / (distance^2 + softening)

Parameters
nametypedefaultdescription
dfpd.DataFrame—OHLCV dataframe. Requires close/volume (price_source "close") or high/low/close/volume (price_source "range").
lookbackint200Number of observations in each rolling window.
price_bins kw-onlyint50Number of price levels in the volume profile.
gravity_constant kw-onlyfloat1.0Gravitational constant G scaling every force.
epsilon kw-onlyfloat1e-09Lower bound for the softening term added to distance^2.
normalize kw-onlyboolTrueIf True, divide the net field by the total absolute force so values land roughly in [-1, 1].
price_source kw-onlyLiteral['close', 'range']'close'"close" assigns each candle's volume to its close bin; "range" distributes it across the bins overlapping the candle's low-high range.
Returns

An IndicatorResult whose values series is aligned to df index, with NaN during the warm-up period.

Raises
ValueErrorIf lookback, price_bins, gravity_constant, epsilon or price_source are out of range.
MissingColumnErrorIf a required column is missing.
InsufficientDataErrorIf df has fewer than lookback rows.
Example
# df: OHLCV dataframe (open, high, low, close, volume)
from market_physics.gravity import gravity_wells

result = gravity_wells(df)
result.name                        # "gravity_wells"
result.metadata["formula"]         # "signed_force = sign(distance) * G * mass / (distance^2 + softening)"
result.values.iloc[-1]             # -0.547603 on the synthetic dataset
result.values.first_valid_index()  # 199 — NaN during warm-up

Reading it — positive pulls upward, negative pulls downward, near zero is balanced

Note — When normalize=True, gravity_constant does not affect the final normalized value.

Limitation — Descriptive inverse-square volume-profile field only. Invalid/no-profile windows (e.g. zero volume, no usable profile, or non-finite current price) return NaN. Not a trading signal, not a support/resistance prediction, not a physical gravity claim, and not a mean-reversion claim.

mass_concentration_score

from market_physics.gravity import mass_concentration_score

mass_concentration_score(
    df: pd.DataFrame,
    lookback: int = 200,
    *,
    price_bins: int = 50,
    price_source: Literal['close', 'range'] = 'range',
    normalize: bool = True,
) -> IndicatorResult

Physical analogy

Volume mass can be tightly clustered in a few price zones or spread thinly across many. Mass Concentration Score summarises that dispersion with a Herfindahl-Hirschman-style concentration measure on the volume profile:

hhi = sum(p_i ** 2)

where p_i is the share of total mass in bin i. When normalised, the score is rescaled so that a perfectly uniform profile maps to 0 and a single-bin profile maps to 1:

normalized = (hhi - 1/k) / (1 - 1/k)

with k = price_bins (the total number of bins). Total bins are used rather than occupied bins so the denominator is stable across rolling windows. Since the minimum achievable hhi over k bins is 1/k (uniform mass), the normalised score stays within [0, 1].

This indicator is descriptive only: it summarises how concentrated volume mass is, not a buy/sell signal.

Interpretation:

  • higher -> mass is concentrated in fewer price zones,
  • lower -> mass is spread across many price zones.

core quantity (sum(p_i ** 2) - 1/k) / (1 - 1/k)

lookbackint200Number of observations in each rolling window (>= 10).
price_bins kw-onlyint50Number of price levels in the volume profile (>= 2).
price_source kw-onlyLiteral['close', 'range']'range'"close" assigns each candle's volume to its close bin; "range" distributes it across the bins overlapping the candle's low-high range.
normalize kw-onlyboolTrueIf True, rescale the index so a uniform profile maps to 0 and a single-bin profile maps to 1.
Returns

from market_physics.gravity import orbital_deviation

orbital_deviation(
    df: pd.DataFrame,
    lookback: int = 200,
    *,
    price_bins: int = 50,
    price_source: Literal['close', 'range'] = 'range',
    center: Literal['dominant', 'center_of_mass'] = 'dominant',
    normalize: bool = True,
    signed: bool = True,
) -> IndicatorResult

Physical analogy

If a high-mass volume zone acts as a gravitational center, the current price can be thought of as a body displaced from that center's "orbit". Orbital Deviation measures that displacement:

deviation = current_close - center_price

where center_price is either the center of the highest-mass bin (center="dominant") or the mass-weighted average of all bin centers (center="center_of_mass"). When normalize is True the deviation is divided by the current close, giving a simple relative displacement. When signed is False the absolute deviation is used.

For each rolling lookback window a volume profile is built over price_bins price levels (see price_source).

This indicator is descriptive only: it summarises how far price sits from a mass center. It makes no mean-reversion claim and implies no expectation that price will move back toward the center.

Interpretation:

  • signed positive -> price is above the mass center,
  • signed negative -> price is below the mass center,
  • magnitude -> distance from the dominant / center-of-mass zone.

core quantity (current_close - center_price) / current_close

fields

Electromagnetism — charge, current, induction · 9 indicators

Electromagnetism is the physics of charge in motion. A static charge creates an electric field (Coulomb); moving charge is a current that creates a magnetic field (Ampère); and a changing magnetic flux induces a voltage that opposes the change that made it (Faraday–Lenz). The fields family maps signed, volume-weighted price motion onto this structure: a bar's return times its relative volume is its charge.

q(t)  =  Σw r·m / Σw |r·m|   — market charge, in [−1, 1]; m = volume ÷ its rolling mean
I(t)  =  Δq / σ(q)   — market current: the rate of change of charge
E(t)  =  meanw(r·m) / stdw(r·m)   — electric field strength

From that one identification the rest of the vocabulary follows. Charge density is the magnitude of that participation — in its default "absolute" mode the rolling mean of |r·m|, how much charge flows regardless of direction; a "signed" mode keeps the net. Polarity is the sign structure of recent moves, the volume-weighted balance of up and down bars: a market flipping between positive and negative charge is depolarised; one accumulating same-signed charge is strongly polarised. The field interaction score is the magnitude of that balance. Current is charge in motion — how fast the charge state changes, standardised by its own rolling volatility — and magnetic flow is the variability of that current: a current that swings around reads strong, a steady one weak. Induction keeps the Faraday idea of coupled changes: the rolling co-movement of the change in relative volume and the change in return, positive when the two rise or fall together and negative when they oppose. Electromagnetic pressure is the composite: the mean of four magnitudes — |charge|, charge density, magnetic flow and |induction| — each mapped into [0, 1], emitted on a bar once at least two of them are defined.

Where the dynamics family asks how price moves, the fields family asks how the volume behind it is charged — its sign, concentration, flow rate, and how those change. Two members coincide with turbulence indicators and their metadata says so: market_charge is the same arithmetic as normalised market_flow, and normalised market_current equals flow_velocity. Every member defaults to a 50-bar window and log returns.

When to reach for this family: pressure and imbalance diagnosis — detecting sustained one-sided, volume-backed motion, polarity flips, and abrupt changes in the charge state.

charge_densityelectric_field_strengthelectromagnetic_pressurefield_interaction_scoremagnetic_flowmarket_chargemarket_currentmarket_inductionpolarity_index

charge_density

from market_physics.fields import charge_density

charge_density(
    df: pd.DataFrame,
    window: int = 50,
    *,
    return_method: Literal['pct', 'log'] = 'log',
    mode: Literal['absolute', 'signed'] = 'absolute',
    normalize: bool = True,
) -> IndicatorResult

This indicator summarises how much signed charge accumulates locally per bar. The per-bar charge contribution is returns * normalized_volume. In "absolute" mode it aggregates the unsigned charge (how much charge is flowing regardless of direction); in "signed" mode it preserves polarity (net charge). Normalised aggregation uses a rolling mean; unnormalised uses a rolling sum.

Known relationship: in signed mode, normalize=False equals market_charge(normalize=False) at matched parameters, and normalize=True is the rolling-mean version of the same signed charge step. It is computed locally and does not import that indicator.

The indicator is a descriptive proxy only: it is an MVP local charge-density feature, not a physical charge density, and not where price will go next.

core quantity rolling_mean(abs(charge_step)); charge_step = returns * normalized_volume

Parameters

dfpd.DataFrame—Dataframe with close and volume columns.
windowint50Lookback window for the rolling aggregation. Must be at least 2.
return_method kw-onlyLiteral['pct', 'log']'log'How to compute returns. "pct" uses percentage change; "log" uses log returns.
mode kw-onlyLiteral['absolute', 'signed']'absolute'"absolute" for unsigned density; "signed" to preserve polarity.
normalize kw-onlyboolTrueIf True, use a rolling mean; otherwise a rolling sum.
Returns

An IndicatorResult aligned to df index, with NaN during the warm-up period and wherever the estimate is undefined.

Raises

result.values.iloc[-1]             # 0.00626814 on the synthetic dataset
result.values.first_valid_index()  # 98 — NaN during warm-up

Reading it — In 'absolute' mode this is the unsigned local charge density (how much charge flows regardless of direction); in 'signed' mode it preserves polarity (net charge). Descriptive only.

from market_physics.fields import electromagnetic_pressure

electromagnetic_pressure(
    df: pd.DataFrame,
    window: int = 50,
    *,
    return_method: Literal['pct', 'log'] = 'log',
    min_valid_components: int = 2,
) -> IndicatorResult

This composite blends four bounded field-interaction magnitudes into a single pressure-like score: the absolute market charge (signed imbalance), the charge density (unsigned magnitude of signed volume participation), the magnetic flow (current variability), and the market induction. Each is mapped into [0, 1] and the score is the mean of the components that are defined.

Because the components are built from progressively deeper rolling constructions (charge, its differenced current, and their rolling statistics), they become valid at different times; a bar is scored only when at least min_valid_components of them are finite.

The indicator is a descriptive composite proxy only: it is not a classifier, not a trading signal, and not a claim about what comes next.

core quantity mean of abs(market_charge), bounded(rolling_mean(abs(charge_step))), bounded(magnetic_flow), and bounded(abs(market_induction)); bounded(x) = abs(x) / (1 + abs(x)); requires at least min_valid_components finite components

waves

Wave physics — Fourier analysis, resonance · 8 indicators

The superposition principle says any signal, however messy, is a sum of pure sinusoids. The discrete Fourier transform makes that decomposition computable: over a rolling window of returns it measures how much of the motion lives at each frequency, and the resulting power spectrum is the market's frequency fingerprint.

X(f) = Σt rt e−2πift   — DFT of the demeaned return window
S(f) ∝ |X(f)|²   — power spectrum: energy per frequency
Hspec = −Σ pf log pf / log K   — spectral entropy: how spread the energy is over the K non-DC frequency bins

Everything in the family is a reading of that spectrum, with the zero-frequency term dropped. The dominant cycle period is the wavelength carrying the most power — the market's strongest rhythm right now, searched between 5 bars and the window length by default. Cycle amplitude is that rhythm's share of the total spectral magnitude; wave energy is the window's total spectral power, or the share inside a chosen period band when one is set. Spectral entropy asks whether the energy is concentrated in a few clean frequencies (an ordered, cyclic market, entropy → 0) or smeared across all of them (noise, entropy → 1). Resonance is the share of total power captured by the single strongest allowed frequency, the way a driven oscillator rings at its natural frequency; frequency pressure is the spectral centroid — where along the frequency axis the power sits. The two paired readings treat price and volume as two coupled oscillators: phase shift is the phase difference between volume changes and returns at the dominant price frequency, and price–volume coherence is the cosine similarity of their power spectra — whether they put their energy at the same frequencies.

Three practical warnings carry over from physics. Fourier analysis assumes the window is quasi-stationary, so regime changes mid-window blur the spectrum. All periods are in bars, not clock time — a dominant cycle of 32 on hourly candles is a 32-hour rhythm. And the transform quantises: a 128-bar window (the default) can only report periods of 128/k bars — 128, 64, 42.7, 32, … — so the dominant period moves in steps, not continuously. A window that contains a single missing or non-finite return, or no variation at all, reads NaN.

When to reach for this family: rhythm detection — whether a cycle exists, how strong it is, and whether price and volume share the same spectral shape and phase.

cycle_amplitudedominant_cycle_periodfrequency_pressurephase_shiftprice_volume_coherenceresonance_scorespectral_entropywave_energy

cycle_amplitude

from market_physics.waves import cycle_amplitude

cycle_amplitude(
    df: pd.DataFrame,
    window: int = 128,
    *,
    return_method: Literal['pct', 'log'] = 'pct',
    min_period: int = 5,
    max_period: int | None = None,
    normalize: bool = True,
) -> IndicatorResult

Physical analogy

Once the strongest cyclic component of recent returns has been identified, its FFT magnitude describes how large that oscillation is. Cycle Amplitude reports the strength of the dominant allowed cycle.

For each rolling window the returns are demeaned and transformed with np.fft.rfft; the zero-frequency (DC) component is dropped. Among the bins whose period falls in [min_period, max_period], the largest magnitude is taken as the dominant amplitude. When normalize is True it is reported as a share of the total non-zero magnitude:

normalized_amplitude = dominant_magnitude / total_nonzero_magnitude

giving a value in [0, 1]. (Magnitude share is used, never power share.)

This indicator is descriptive only: it summarises the strength of the dominant recent cycle, not a buy/sell signal.

Interpretation:

  • higher -> the dominant cycle accounts for more of the recent oscillation,
  • lower -> oscillation is spread more evenly across cycles.

core quantity dominant_magnitude = max(|rfft(demeaned_returns)|) over [min_period, max_period]; normalized = dominant_magnitude / total_nonzero_magnitude

Parameters
nametypedefaultdescription
dfpd.DataFrame—OHLCV dataframe. Only the close column is required.
windowint128Number of observations in each rolling FFT window (>= 8).
return_method kw-onlyLiteral['pct', 'log']'pct'How to compute returns. "pct" uses percentage change; "log" uses log returns.
min_period kw-onlyint5Shortest cycle period considered, in bars (>= 2).
max_period kw-onlyint | NoneNoneLongest cycle period considered, in bars. None imposes no upper bound; when provided it must satisfy min_period < max_period <= window.
normalize kw-onlyboolTrueIf True, report the dominant magnitude as a share of the total non-zero magnitude (a value in [0, 1]); if False, report the raw dominant magnitude.
Returns

An IndicatorResult aligned to df index, with NaN during the warm-up period and for windows with no resolvable cycle.

Raises
ValueErrorIf window, return_method, min_period or max_period is out of range.
MissingColumnErrorIf the close column is missing.
InsufficientDataErrorIf df has fewer than window + 1 rows.
Example
# df: OHLCV dataframe (open, high, low, close, volume)
from market_physics.waves import cycle_amplitude

result = cycle_amplitude(df)
result.name                        # "cycle_amplitude"
result.metadata["formula"]         # "dominant_magnitude = max(|rfft(demeaned_returns)|) over [min_period, max_period]; normalized = dominant_magnitude / total_nonzero_magnit..."
result.values.iloc[-1]             # 0.0496499 on the synthetic dataset
result.values.first_valid_index()  # 128 — NaN during warm-up

Reading it — higher means the dominant cycle accounts for more of the recent oscillation, lower means oscillation is spread across cycles

Related — Magnitude-share sibling of resonance_score; both use the same dominant spectral bin and typically correlate highly, while cycle_amplitude uses magnitude share and resonance_score uses power share.

Limitation — FFT resolution is limited by window length; periods are in bars, not clock time; assumes stationarity within the window; descriptive only

from market_physics.waves import dominant_cycle_period

dominant_cycle_period(
    df: pd.DataFrame,
    window: int = 128,
    *,
    return_method: Literal['pct', 'log'] = 'pct',
    min_period: int = 5,
    max_period: int | None = None,
) -> IndicatorResult

Physical analogy

A price series can be treated as a superposition of oscillations. Decomposing the recent returns with a discrete Fourier transform reveals which cyclic component carries the most power. The Dominant Cycle Period reports the length (in bars) of that strongest cycle.

For each rolling window the returns are demeaned, transformed with np.fft.rfft, and the zero-frequency (DC) component is dropped. Frequencies are converted to periods via period = 1 / frequency (so periods are measured in bars), filtered to [min_period, max_period], and the period with the maximum power is returned.

This indicator is descriptive only: it summarises the length of the strongest recent cycle, not a buy/sell signal, and implies no prediction that the cycle will persist.

Interpretation:

  • larger value -> the strongest recent oscillation is a longer (slower) cycle,
  • smaller value -> the strongest recent oscillation is a shorter (faster) cycle.

core quantity period = 1 / argmax_frequency(power_spectrum(demeaned_returns)); DC ignored; restricted to [min_period, max_period]

from market_physics.waves import frequency_pressure

frequency_pressure(
    df: pd.DataFrame,
    window: int = 128,
    *,
    return_method: Literal['pct', 'log'] = 'pct',
    normalize: bool = True,
) -> IndicatorResult

Physical analogy

The spectral centroid is the "center of mass" of a power spectrum along the frequency axis. Frequency Pressure reports that centroid for recent returns: it shifts toward higher frequencies when energy sits in faster oscillations and toward lower frequencies when energy sits in slower ones.

For each rolling window the returns are demeaned and transformed with np.fft.rfft; the zero-frequency (DC) component is dropped and the power spectrum is formed. The centroid is:

centroid = sum(frequency * power) / sum(power)

measured in cycles per bar. When normalize is True it is divided by the highest non-DC frequency present in the window, giving a value in [0, 1].

This indicator is descriptive only: it summarises where spectral energy sits along the frequency axis, not a buy/sell signal.

Interpretation:

  • higher (normalised) -> more energy in faster oscillations,
  • lower (normalised) -> more energy in slower oscillations.

core quantity centroid = sum(frequency * power) / sum(power) (DC ignored); normalized = centroid / max_frequency

from market_physics.waves import phase_shift

phase_shift(
    df: pd.DataFrame,
    window: int = 128,
    *,
    return_method: Literal['pct', 'log'] = 'pct',
    min_period: int = 5,
    max_period: int | None = None,
    degrees: bool = True,
) -> IndicatorResult

Physical analogy

Two oscillations at the same frequency can be offset in phase. Phase Shift reports the phase relation between volume participation and price movement at the dominant price frequency of a rolling window.

For each rolling window the price signal (close returns) and the volume signal (volume percentage changes) are demeaned and transformed with np.fft.rfft; the zero-frequency (DC) component is dropped. The dominant price frequency within [min_period, max_period] is located, and the phase difference at that frequency bin k is:

phase_difference = angle(volume_fft[k]) - angle(price_fft[k])

wrapped to [-pi, pi] (converted to degrees when degrees is True).

This is a descriptive phase relation only — it is not a predictive lead/lag signal and makes no claim that volume leads or predicts price. It is descriptive only, not a buy/sell signal.

Interpretation:

  • the value describes the phase relation between volume and price movement at the dominant price frequency,
  • a non-zero value describes an offset in that shared oscillation; it carries no predictive lead/lag meaning.

core quantity phase = wrap(angle(volume_fft[k]) - angle(price_fft[k])) at the dominant price frequency k within [min_period, max_period]

min_period kw-onlyint5Shortest cycle period considered, in bars (>= 2).
max_period kw-onlyint | NoneNoneLongest cycle period considered, in bars. None imposes no upper bound; when provided it must satisfy min_period < max_period <= window.
degrees kw-onlyboolTrueIf True, report the phase difference in degrees ([-180, 180]); if False, in radians ([-pi, pi]).

from market_physics.waves import price_volume_coherence

price_volume_coherence(
    df: pd.DataFrame,
    window: int = 128,
    *,
    return_method: Literal['pct', 'log'] = 'pct',

Physical analogy

Two oscillating systems are "coherent" when their energy is distributed across frequencies in a similar way. Price-Volume Coherence compares the spectral power distribution of price movement with that of volume participation: it is high when both concentrate their oscillation energy at the same frequencies and low when they do not.

For each rolling window the price signal (close returns) and the volume signal (volume percentage changes) are demeaned and transformed with np.fft.rfft. The zero-frequency (DC) component is dropped, each power spectrum is normalised into a distribution, and the coherence is their cosine similarity, giving a value in [0, 1].

This is a coherence-style proxy, not scipy.signal.coherence. It is descriptive only: it summarises how similar the two spectral shapes are, not a buy/sell signal.

Interpretation:

  • higher -> price movement and volume participation have more similar spectral power distributions,
  • lower -> less similar spectral power distributions.

from market_physics.waves import resonance_score

resonance_score(

Physical analogy

A resonant system concentrates its energy at a single frequency. The Resonance Score measures how much of the recent spectral power is captured by the single strongest allowed frequency:

resonance = dominant_band_power / total_nonzero_power

For each rolling window the returns are demeaned and transformed with np.fft.rfft; the zero-frequency (DC) component is dropped and the power spectrum is formed. Among the bins whose period falls in [min_period, max_period], the largest power is the dominant band power; the denominator is the total power across all non-DC bins. The result lies in [0, 1].

This indicator is descriptive only: it summarises how concentrated recent spectral power is at one frequency, not a buy/sell signal. It makes no claim that the resonance will persist.

Interpretation:

  • higher -> one allowed frequency explains a larger share of recent spectral power,
  • lower -> power is spread more evenly across frequencies.

core quantity resonance = max(power over [min_period, max_period]) / total_nonzero_power (DC ignored)

    *,
    return_method: Literal['pct', 'log'] = 'pct',
    base: float = 2.0,
    normalize: bool = True,
) -> IndicatorResult

Physical analogy

Treating recent returns as a signal, the power spectrum describes how energy is distributed across frequencies. Spectral Entropy applies Shannon entropy to that (normalised) power spectrum: it is low when energy concentrates in a few frequencies and high when energy is spread evenly across many.

For each rolling window the returns are demeaned and transformed with np.fft.rfft; the zero-frequency (DC) component is dropped and the power spectrum is converted to a probability distribution p_i. The entropy is:

H = -sum(p_i * log_b(p_i))

optionally divided by log_b(n_frequencies) (the number of non-DC frequency bins) to give a value in [0, 1].

This indicator is descriptive only: it summarises how dispersed the return spectrum is, not a buy/sell signal.

Interpretation:

  • low -> spectrum concentrated in fewer frequencies,
  • high -> spectrum more dispersed / noisy.

core quantity H = -sum(p_i * log_b(p_i)); p_i = power_i / total_power (DC ignored); normalized H = H / log_b(n_frequencies)

Parameters
nametypedefaultdescription
dfpd.DataFrame—OHLCV dataframe. Only the close column is required.
windowint128Number of observations in each rolling FFT window (>= 8).
return_method kw-onlyLiteral['pct', 'log']'pct'How to compute returns. "pct" uses percentage change; "log" uses log returns.
base kw-onlyfloat2.0Logarithm base for the entropy (> 1). 2 gives bits.
normalize kw-onlyboolTrueIf True, divide the entropy by log_b(n_frequencies) so values land in [0, 1].
Returns

An IndicatorResult aligned to df index, with NaN during the warm-up period and for windows with no resolvable spectrum.

Raises
ValueErrorIf window, base or return_method is out of range.
MissingColumnErrorIf the close column is missing.
InsufficientDataErrorIf df has fewer than window + 1 rows (the first return is NaN, so a full valid window needs one extra row).
Example
# df: OHLCV dataframe (open, high, low, close, volume)
from market_physics.waves import spectral_entropy

result = spectral_entropy(df)
result.name                        # "spectral_entropy"
result.metadata["formula"]         # "H = -sum(p_i * log_b(p_i)); p_i = power_i / total_power (DC ignored); normalized H = H / log_b(n_frequencies)"
result.values.iloc[-1]             # 0.881604 on the synthetic dataset
result.values.first_valid_index()  # 128 — NaN during warm-up

Reading it — low means the spectrum is concentrated in fewer frequencies, high means it is more dispersed / noisy

Limitation — FFT resolution is limited by window length; frequencies are per bar, not clock time; assumes stationarity within the window; descriptive only

from market_physics.waves import wave_energy

wave_energy(
    df: pd.DataFrame,
    window: int = 128,
    *,
    return_method: Literal['pct', 'log'] = 'pct',
    min_period: int | None = None,
    max_period: int | None = None,
    normalize: bool = True,
) -> IndicatorResult

Physical analogy

By Parseval's relation, the power spectrum of a signal distributes its energy across frequencies. Wave Energy measures the spectral energy of recent returns, optionally restricted to a band of cycle periods.

For each rolling window the returns are demeaned and transformed with np.fft.rfft; the zero-frequency (DC) component is dropped and the power spectrum |rfft|^2 is formed. Behaviour depends on whether a period band is provided (i.e. at least one of min_period/max_period is set):

  • With a band and normalize=True: the reported value is the selected band power divided by the total non-zero power, a share in [0, 1].
  • With a band and normalize=False: the raw summed band power.
  • Without a band: the raw total non-zero spectral energy, even when normalize=True — normalisation is not applicable without a band and is ignored.

This indicator is descriptive only: it summarises spectral energy, not a buy/sell signal.

Interpretation:

  • higher -> more oscillation energy (in the band, if one is given),
  • lower -> less oscillation energy.

core quantity power = |rfft(demeaned_returns)|^2 (DC ignored); band power / total_nonzero_power when a band is normalised, otherwise raw summed power

Parameters

dfpd.DataFrame—OHLCV dataframe. Only the close column is required.
windowint128Number of observations in each rolling FFT window (>= 8).
return_method kw-onlyLiteral['pct', 'log']'pct'How to compute returns. "pct" uses percentage change; "log" uses log returns.
min_period kw-onlyint | NoneNoneShortest cycle period in the band, in bars (>= 2 when provided).
max_period kw-onlyint | NoneNoneLongest cycle period in the band, in bars (<= window when provided). When both bounds are provided they must satisfy min_period < max_period.
normalize kw-onlyboolTrueIf True and a period band is provided, report the band power as a share of the total non-zero power (a value in [0, 1]). Ignored when no band is provided.

result.values.iloc[-1]             # 0.389837 on the synthetic dataset
result.values.first_valid_index()  # 128 — NaN during warm-up

turbulence

Fluid dynamics — flow, vorticity, cascades · 9 indicators

Fluid dynamics distinguishes two states of flow. Laminar flow is smooth and layered — a river gliding through a straight channel. Turbulent flow is churning and eddying — the same river through rapids. Which state a fluid occupies is governed by the Reynolds number, the ratio of inertial to viscous forces; and once flow turns turbulent, Kolmogorov's 1941 theory describes what happens: energy injected at large scales cascades down through eddies of smaller and smaller size until viscosity dissipates it as heat.

Re = ρvL/μ   — inertia vs. viscosity: laminar below, turbulent above
E(k) ∝ k−5/3   — Kolmogorov cascade: energy spectrum across eddy scales
I = σv / v̄   — turbulence intensity: fluctuation over mean flow
st = rt · mt   — the market's flow step: return × relative volume (volume ÷ its rolling mean)

The market analogue treats directional price movement as flow and volatility as its turbulent fluctuation. The flow readings are built from the per-bar flow step above (six of the nine members accept volume_weighted=False to drop the weight); the volatility cascade reads plain returns. Market flow is the net of those steps as a fraction of their total magnitude, in [−1, 1]; flow velocity is how fast that level changes, standardised by its own variability. Turbulence intensity adapts the engineering ratio: the dispersion of the flow steps relative to their typical magnitude. A trending, low-volatility market is laminar; a violent, directionless one is turbulent. Vorticity captures local rotation, measured as the rate at which consecutive flow steps reverse sign, in [0, 1]. Viscosity is the market's internal friction: the share of the flow path that cancels out instead of producing net displacement. The volatility cascade borrows Kolmogorov's idea at two scales: it compares short-scale volatility (20 bars) with a longer baseline (100 bars), as a ratio or a difference — a two-point comparison, not an estimate of a spectral cascade. Eddy pressure (vorticity × intensity) and the two composites, the flow instability score and the turbulent regime score, summarise where the tape sits on the laminar–turbulent spectrum.

Several members coincide with indicators in other families, and the metadata says so at matched parameters: volatility_cascade in ratio mode is dynamics' damping_ratio, unweighted market_viscosity is dynamics' market_friction, and weighted market_viscosity is 1 − |market_flow| — thermodynamics' heat_dissipation computes the same quantity again. The family defaults to log returns and a 50-bar window (100 for the cascade and the two composites), while dynamics defaults to percentage returns, so a comparison needs both set explicitly.

When to reach for this family: volatility-regime diagnosis with directionality kept in the picture — not just "is volatility high" but "is the flow smooth or churning, and is short-scale volatility running above or below its longer baseline".

eddy_pressureflow_instability_scoreflow_velocityflow_vorticitymarket_flowmarket_viscosityturbulence_intensityturbulent_regime_scorevolatility_cascade

from market_physics.turbulence import eddy_pressure

eddy_pressure(
    df: pd.DataFrame,
    window: int = 50,
    *,
    return_method: Literal['pct', 'log'] = 'log',
    volume_weighted: bool = True,
) -> IndicatorResult

Eddy Pressure is the fluid-dynamics analogue of the agitation carried by eddies in a turbulent flow. It combines two descriptive proxies computed from the same (optionally volume-weighted) flow steps:

  • vorticity — the rolling rate of flow-step sign changes (how often the flow reverses direction), and
  • intensity — the rolling dispersion of the flow steps relative to their typical magnitude (rolling_std / rolling_mean(abs)).

eddy_pressure = vorticity * intensity

Higher values describe flow that both reverses often and fluctuates strongly in magnitude; lower values describe smoother, steadier flow. This is a descriptive feature only — it is not a trading signal and carries no directional recommendation.

core quantity eddy_pressure = vorticity * intensity

windowint50Rolling window for both components (>= 2).
return_method kw-onlyLiteral['pct', 'log']'log'How to compute returns. "pct" uses percentage change; "log" uses log returns.
volume_weighted kw-onlyboolTrueIf True, weight each flow step by rolling_normalized_volume(volume, window).
Returns

An IndicatorResult aligned to df index, with NaN during the warm-up period and wherever either component is undefined.

Raises
ValueErrorIf window is less than 2 or return_method is invalid.
MissingColumnErrorIf close is missing, or volume is missing when volume_weighted is True.
InsufficientDataErrorIf df has fewer rows than needed for one defined output (2 * window - 1 when volume-weighted, window + 1 otherwise).
Example
# df: OHLCV dataframe (open, high, low, close, volume)
from market_physics.turbulence import eddy_pressure

result = eddy_pressure(df)
result.name                        # "eddy_pressure"
result.metadata["formula"]         # "eddy_pressure = vorticity * intensity"
result.values.iloc[-1]             # 0.559391 on the synthetic dataset
result.values.first_valid_index()  # 98 — NaN during warm-up

Reading it — Higher values describe flow that both reverses often and fluctuates strongly in magnitude; lower values describe smoother, steadier flow. Descriptive only — not a signal.

Limitation — A composite proxy multiplying a sign-change-rate rotation proxy by a dispersion-ratio intensity proxy; it does not model true eddy pressure and does not predict future price direction.

from market_physics.turbulence import flow_instability_score

flow_instability_score(
    df: pd.DataFrame,
    window: int = 100,
    *,
    return_method: Literal['pct', 'log'] = 'log',
    volume_weighted: bool = True,
) -> IndicatorResult

Flow Instability Score is a composite descriptive proxy that averages three turbulence-inspired characteristics of the (optionally volume-weighted) flow steps over a window:

  • vorticity — the rolling rate of flow-step sign changes (how often the flow reverses direction),
  • intensity — the rolling dispersion of the flow steps relative to their typical magnitude (rolling_std / rolling_mean(abs)), and
  • acceleration — the typical bar-to-bar change in the flow steps relative to their typical magnitude (rolling_mean(abs(diff)) / rolling_mean(abs)).

The score is the row-wise mean of whichever components are finite, and is NaN when too few components are defined. Higher values describe flow that reverses, disperses and jerks more; lower values describe steadier flow. This is a descriptive composite proxy only — it is not a trading signal and carries no directional recommendation.

core quantity score = mean of the finite components {vorticity, intensity, acceleration}
