from market_physics.chaos import local_divergence_pressure

local_divergence_pressure(
    df: pd.DataFrame,
    window: int = 512,
    *,
    short_window: int = 128,
    source: Literal['returns', 'close'] = 'returns',
    return_method: Literal['pct', 'log'] = 'log',
    embedding_dimension: int = 3,
    delay: int = 1,
    horizon: int = 1,
) -> IndicatorResult

This indicator compares the Lyapunov-style local divergence over the most recent short_window bars against a baseline built from the same window geometry: the full window is split into non-overlapping short_window segments, the local divergence is estimated on each, and the baseline is their mean. The pressure is the signed difference between the recent divergence and that baseline. Matching the window sizes keeps the estimator's finite-sample behaviour consistent, so a homogeneous window centres the pressure near zero.

The divergence estimates use min_neighbors=1 so they stay defined on the short segments involved; they can therefore be noisier than the standalone lyapunov_proxy.

The indicator is a descriptive proxy only: it summarises how recent local divergence compares with the segmented baseline, not where price will go and not the presence of chaos.

core quantity short_divergence - long_divergence; short_divergence is the local divergence of the most recent short_window returns and long_divergence is the mean over non-overlapping short_window segments of the full window

from market_physics.chaos import lyapunov_proxy

In nonlinear dynamics the largest Lyapunov exponent measures how fast nearby trajectories in state space separate over time. This indicator computes a lightweight proxy in the same spirit: it embeds a rolling window into a time-delay phase space, pairs each state with its nearest non-adjacent neighbour, and averages how much those pairs separate over a short horizon.

The indicator is a descriptive proxy only: a positive value means nearby states tended to diverge over the horizon and a negative value means they tended to converge. It is not a rigorous Lyapunov exponent and does not prove the presence of chaos.

from market_physics.chaos import phase_space_density

phase_space_density(
    df: pd.DataFrame,
    window: int = 256,
    *,
    source: Literal['returns', 'close'] = 'returns',
    return_method: Literal['pct', 'log'] = 'log',
    embedding_dimension: int = 3,
    delay: int = 1,

This indicator reports how compactly the reconstructed phase-space trajectory packs together, relative to its own scale. For each embedded state it measures the distance to its nearest neighbour; a cloud whose states sit close to one another (small nearest-neighbour distances relative to the cloud's spread) reads as denser.

Unlike a recurrence rate, this proxy needs no recurrence radius: it compares the mean nearest-neighbour distance against the embedding scale directly, so it is a genuinely distinct quantity rather than a thresholded pair count.

The indicator is a descriptive MVP proxy only: it summarises how compact the reconstructed state cloud is, not where price will go and not the presence of chaos.

from market_physics.chaos import recurrence_determinism

recurrence_determinism(
    df: pd.DataFrame,
    window: int = 256,
    *,
    source: Literal['returns', 'close'] = 'returns',
    return_method: Literal['pct', 'log'] = 'log',
    embedding_dimension: int = 3,
    delay: int = 1,
    radius: float | None = None,
    radius_quantile: float = 0.1,
    min_line_length: int = 2,
) -> IndicatorResult

Recurrence quantification analysis calls a system's behaviour more deterministic when its recurrences line up into diagonal structures: nearby trajectories that stay close for several steps trace parallel lines in the recurrence matrix, whereas isolated recurrences scatter as single points. This indicator reports the fraction of recurrent points that belong to diagonal lines of at least min_line_length.

The indicator is a descriptive MVP RQA-style proxy only: it summarises how much of the reconstructed recurrence structure is organised into diagonal lines, not where price will go and not the presence of chaos.

Radius policy (deliberate, do not "harmonize" with recurrence_rate): this structure metric uses a quantile-calibrated radius. Fixing the recurrence density to a quantile makes diagonal-line structure comparable across windows, and the determinism ratio still depends on the data even at a pinned density. recurrence_rate instead uses a scale-adaptive radius on purpose, because a quantile radius would make the reported rate circular (equal to the quantile by construction).

core quantity points on diagonal lines (length >= min_line_length) / total off-diagonal recurrent points

The indicator is a descriptive MVP RQA-style proxy only: it summarises the complexity of the reconstructed recurrence structure, not where price will go and not the presence of chaos.

from market_physics.chaos import recurrence_rate

recurrence_rate(
    df: pd.DataFrame,

Recurrence quantification analysis asks how often a dynamical system revisits neighbourhoods of its past states. This indicator embeds a rolling window into a time-delay phase space and reports the fraction of distinct state pairs that fall within a recurrence radius. A higher rate means the reconstructed trajectory revisits similar states more often.

By default the radius adapts to the scale of the embedded state cloud (radius_scale times the mean per-coordinate standard deviation), so the reported rate reflects the actual geometry of the window. It is deliberately not calibrated to a quantile of the same window's distances, which would force the rate to a fixed target regardless of the data.

The indicator is a descriptive proxy only: it summarises how recurrent the reconstructed state cloud is, not where price will go and not the presence of chaos.

fractals

Fractal geometry — Hurst scaling, multifractality · 9 indicators

Fractal geometry entered finance through finance itself: Mandelbrot's 1963 study of cotton prices found that their fluctuations look statistically identical at every zoom level — self-similarity — and that this scaling is quantifiable. The central exponent is Hurst's H, originally invented for Nile flood records:

std(xt+ℓ − xt) ∝ ℓH   — lagged-difference scaling: H>½ persistent, H<½ anti-persistent, H=½ random walk
Var(sum of s returns) ∝ s2H   — variance of aggregates: the exponent is ≈ 1 for uncorrelated returns
D ≈ 2 − H   — fractal dimension of a self-affine path

H = 0.5 is the random-walk fingerprint. Above it, moves tend to be followed by moves the same way — long-memory persistence; below it, the path anti-persists, reverting more than chance allows. The Hurst exponent estimates this directly — not through Hurst's own rescaled range but as the log-log slope of lagged-difference dispersion against lag, measured by default on each window's demeaned cumulative return path; the variance scaling exponent measures the same thing through the variance-of-aggregates route, and reports the exponent of that law itself, so an uncorrelated series reads near 1 rather than ½. Fractal dimension (the Katz estimator) and the roughness index read the geometry of the path itself — a smooth trending line has dimension near 1 and the value rises as the path grows more jagged (the Katz estimator is not capped at 2 and runs well above it on noise-dominated windows), while roughness runs from 0 for a perfectly direct path to 1 for pure back-and-forth. Long memory scores how much autocorrelation survives across lags: the mean absolute autocorrelation over lags 1–20, taken on absolute returns by default, so it measures volatility persistence unless pointed at raw returns.

The multifractal pair generalises: real markets are rarely monofractal — small fluctuations and large ones scale with different exponents. The generalized Hurst exponent H(q) measures scaling at each moment order q, and the multifractal spectrum width summarises how much H(q) varies — max H(q) − min H(q) over q = 1, 2, 3 by default, a spread-of-exponents proxy rather than a full singularity spectrum; wide spreads are the classic signature of intermittent dynamics. Two readings watch the scaling law itself. Scaling stability asks whether the lower and upper bands of aggregation scales agree on the variance exponent within one window, 1 / (1 + |βlow − βhigh|); local scaling pressure compares the exponent of the most recent 128 bars with its mean over the non-overlapping 128-bar segments of a 512-bar window — whether recent scaling has moved off its own baseline.

When to reach for this family: memory and roughness measurement — whether the series trends, reverts, or diffuses, and whether that behaviour is uniform across scales or intermittent.

from market_physics.fractals import fractal_dimension

fractal_dimension(
    df: pd.DataFrame,
    window: int = 256,
    *,
    source_column: str = 'close',
) -> IndicatorResult

Fractal Dimension indicator (Katz estimator).

The fractal dimension of a curve describes how completely it fills the space between its points: a smooth line has dimension close to 1, while an extremely irregular, jagged path approaches 2. The Katz estimator expresses this through the ratio between the total path length of the series and its maximum extent from the first point.

The indicator is a descriptive geometry proxy only: it quantifies how jagged the recent price path has been, not where price will go next.

from market_physics.fractals import generalized_hurst_exponent

generalized_hurst_exponent(
    df: pd.DataFrame,

The generalized Hurst exponent H(q) extends the single Hurst exponent to a family indexed by the moment order q: instead of only the second-moment dispersion, it measures how the q-th order absolute moment of lagged differences scales with the lag. Different q emphasise different sizes of fluctuation, so the way H(q) varies with q is a fingerprint of multifractal structure.

This is an MVP multifractal-style estimator, not the full multifractal formalism. The indicator is descriptive only: it characterises scaling behaviour for a chosen fluctuation order and is not a directional signal.

from market_physics.fractals import hurst_exponent

hurst_exponent(
    df: pd.DataFrame,
    window: int = 256,
    *,
    source: Literal['close', 'returns'] = 'returns',
    return_method: Literal['pct', 'log'] = 'log',
    min_lag: int = 2,
    max_lag: int | None = None,
) -> IndicatorResult

The Hurst exponent comes from the study of long-range dependence in stochastic processes and fractal time series: it describes how the dispersion of increments scales with the time lag over which they are measured. For a self-similar process, std(x[t + lag] - x[t]) grows like lag ** H. The scaling law applies to a path (a cumulative process), so when the source is a returns series the estimator first rebuilds a cumulative path from the demeaned returns of each window before measuring the scaling.

Market interpretation of the rolling estimate H:

  • H > 0.5 — persistent-like structure (increments tend to keep their recent character),
  • H around 0.5 — random-walk-like scaling,
  • H < 0.5 — anti-persistent-like structure (increments tend to alternate).

The indicator is a descriptive estimator only: it characterises the scaling structure of the observed series and is not a directional signal.

core quantity log(std(diff_lag)) ~ H * log(lag) over lags in [min_lag, max_lag]; for source='returns' the scaling is measured on the cumulative sum of the demeaned returns window

min_lag kw-onlyint2Smallest lag (in bars) used in the scaling fit. At least 2.
max_lag kw-onlyint | NoneNoneLargest lag used in the scaling fit. Defaults to window // 4 when None (large lags leave few lagged differences per window and bias the estimate); an explicit value must satisfy min_lag < max_lag <= window // 2.

from market_physics.fractals import local_scaling_pressure

local_scaling_pressure(
    df: pd.DataFrame,
    window: int = 512,
    *,
    short_window: int = 128,
    return_method: Literal['pct', 'log'] = 'log',
    min_scale: int = 2,
    max_scale: int | None = None,
) -> IndicatorResult

Local Scaling Pressure compares how returns scale over the most recent short_window bars against a baseline built from the same window geometry: the full window is split into non-overlapping short_window segments, a variance-scaling exponent is estimated on each, and the baseline is their mean. The pressure is the signed difference between the most recent segment's exponent and that baseline. Matching the window sizes keeps the finite-sample bias of the non-overlapping block-sum estimator consistent between the local and baseline estimates, so homogeneous scaling data centres the pressure near zero.

The physical analogy is loose: like a pressure difference between two regions, a positive value means the recent local scaling sits above the segmented baseline and a negative value means it sits below.

This is an MVP proxy built from coarse variance-scaling slopes, not a formal scaling-regime test. The indicator is descriptive only and is not a directional signal.

core quantity beta_short - beta_long; beta_short is the variance-scaling exponent of the most recent short_window returns and beta_long is the mean exponent over non-overlapping short_window segments of the full window

from market_physics.fractals import multifractal_spectrum_width

multifractal_spectrum_width(
    df: pd.DataFrame,
    window: int = 512,
    *,
    q_values: Sequence[float] = (1.0, 2.0, 3.0),
    return_method: Literal['pct', 'log'] = 'log',
    min_lag: int = 2,
    max_lag: int | None = None,
) -> IndicatorResult

A monofractal series scales the same way regardless of the moment order used to probe it, so its generalized Hurst exponents H(q) are all roughly equal. A multifractal series scales differently for small and large fluctuations, so H(q) spreads out across q. The width of that spread is a compact proxy for how multifractal the recent series looks.

This is an MVP proxy based on the spread of generalized Hurst exponents, not the full multifractal formalism (no formal singularity spectrum). The indicator is descriptive only and is not a directional signal.

core quantity max(H(q_values)) - min(H(q_values))

Parameters
nametypedefaultdescription
dfpd.DataFrame—Dataframe with a close column.
windowint512Lookback window for the rolling estimate. Must be at least 64.
q_values kw-onlySequence[float](1.0, 2.0, 3.0)Moment orders to probe. At least two distinct, finite, strictly positive values.
return_method kw-onlyLiteral['pct', 'log']'log'How to compute returns. "pct" uses percentage change; "log" uses log returns.
min_lag kw-onlyint2Smallest lag (in bars) used in each scaling fit. At least 2.
max_lag kw-onlyint | NoneNoneLargest lag used in each scaling fit. Defaults to window // 4 when None; an explicit value must satisfy min_lag < max_lag <= window // 2.
Returns

An IndicatorResult aligned to df index, with non-negative values, NaN during the warm-up period and wherever any H(q) is undefined.

Raises
ValueErrorIf q_values, window, return_method or the lag bounds are invalid.
MissingColumnErrorIf close is missing.
InsufficientDataErrorIf df has fewer than window + 1 rows (returns lose the first row).
Example

from market_physics.fractals import multifractal_spectrum_width

result.name                        # "multifractal_spectrum_width"

result.values.iloc[-1]             # 0.0938431 on the synthetic dataset
result.values.first_valid_index()  # 512 — NaN during warm-up

Reading it — Higher width indicates more heterogeneous scaling behaviour across moment orders q; lower width indicates more uniform scaling. Descriptive proxy only.

Limitation — MVP proxy based on spread of generalized Hurst exponents; not a full multifractal formalism

from market_physics.fractals import roughness_index

roughness_index(
    df: pd.DataFrame,
    window: int = 100,
    *,
    source_column: str = 'close',
    normalize: bool = True,
) -> IndicatorResult

The roughness of a path compares how far the series travelled in total with how far it actually got: a perfectly efficient path covers its net displacement with no wasted motion, while a rough path wanders back and forth, accumulating path length without displacement. This mirrors the tortuosity of a curve in fractal geometry.

The indicator is a descriptive path-geometry proxy only: it quantifies how indirect the recent price path has been, not where price will go next.

core quantity 1 - |x[-1] - x[0]| / sum(|diff(x)|), clipped to [0, 1]

windowint100Lookback window for the rolling estimate. Must be at least 2.

normalize kw-onlyboolTrueIf True, bound the roughness into [0, 1].
Returns

An IndicatorResult aligned to df index, with NaN during the warm-up period and wherever the estimate is undefined.

Raises
ValueErrorIf window is less than 2.
MissingColumnErrorIf source_column is missing.
InsufficientDataErrorIf df has fewer than window rows.
Example

from market_physics.fractals import scaling_stability

scaling_stability(
    df: pd.DataFrame,
    window: int = 256,
    *,
    return_method: Literal['pct', 'log'] = 'log',
    min_scale: int = 2,
    max_scale: int | None = None,
) -> IndicatorResult

A well-behaved scaling regime would show a consistent variance-scaling exponent regardless of which band of aggregation scales is measured. This indicator compares the variance-scaling exponent estimated on the lower band of scales with the one estimated on the upper band and reports how close the two are.

This is an MVP consistency proxy, not a formal test or proof of a scaling regime: agreement between two coarse slope estimates is suggestive, not conclusive. The indicator is descriptive only and is not a directional signal.

core quantity 1 / (1 + abs(beta_low_scales - beta_high_scales))

Parameters
nametypedefaultdescription
dfpd.DataFrame—Dataframe with a close column.
windowint256Lookback window for the rolling estimate. Must be at least 64 so the default scale range still splits into two bands.
return_method kw-onlyLiteral['pct', 'log']'log'How to compute returns. "pct" uses percentage change; "log" uses log returns.
min_scale kw-onlyint2Smallest aggregation scale (in bars). At least 2.
max_scale kw-onlyint | NoneNoneLargest aggregation scale. Defaults to window // 8 when None (about eight non-overlapping blocks at the largest default scale); an explicit value must satisfy min_scale < max_scale <= window // 2 and leave at least four scales so each band holds at least two. Larger ceilings leave few blocks at the top scale and bias the per-band estimates downward.
Returns

An IndicatorResult aligned to df index, with values in [0, 1], NaN during the warm-up period and wherever the proxy is undefined.

Raises
ValueErrorIf window, return_method or the scale bounds are invalid, or the resolved scale range holds fewer than four scales.
MissingColumnErrorIf close is missing.
InsufficientDataErrorIf df has fewer than window + 1 rows (returns lose the first row).
Example
# df: OHLCV dataframe (open, high, low, close, volume)
from market_physics.fractals import scaling_stability

result = scaling_stability(df)
result.name                        # "scaling_stability"
result.metadata["formula"]         # "1 / (1 + abs(beta_low_scales - beta_high_scales))"
result.values.iloc[-1]             # 0.437671 on the synthetic dataset
result.values.first_valid_index()  # 256 — NaN during warm-up

Reading it — Values closer to 1 indicate more stable scaling estimates across scale bands; values closer to 0 indicate inconsistent scaling across scale bands. Descriptive proxy only.

Limitation — MVP proxy based on consistency of variance-scaling slopes across scale bands; not a formal proof of a scaling regime. Large scales use fewer non-overlapping blocks, and a large max_scale can bias the per-band estimates downward; sensitive to window and scale choices.

from market_physics.fractals import variance_scaling_exponent

variance_scaling_exponent(
    df: pd.DataFrame,
    window: int = 256,
    *,
    return_method: Literal['pct', 'log'] = 'log',
    min_scale: int = 2,
    max_scale: int | None = None,
) -> IndicatorResult

In the study of self-similar processes, the variance of aggregated increments grows as a power law of the aggregation scale: var(sum over scale) ~ scale ** beta. For an uncorrelated (Brownian) process the exponent is beta ~ 1; persistent aggregation grows faster and anti-persistent aggregation grows more slowly.

The indicator is a descriptive estimator only: it characterises how the variance of block-aggregated returns scales with block size and is not a directional signal.

core quantity log(var(aggregated_returns_scale)) ~ beta * log(scale)

max_scale kw-onlyint | NoneNoneLargest aggregation scale. Defaults to window // 8 when None (about eight non-overlapping blocks at the largest default scale); an explicit value must satisfy min_scale < max_scale <= window // 2. Larger ceilings leave few blocks at the top scale and bias the estimate downward.
Returns

An IndicatorResult aligned to df index, with NaN during the warm-up period and wherever the estimate is undefined.

networks

Network physics & random matrix theory · 9 indicators

A market of many assets is a many-body system, and its interaction structure lives in the correlation matrix. Econophysics' landmark result (Laloux et al.; Plerou et al., 1999) is that most of that matrix is noise — and that the noise is exactly characterisable. Random matrix theory gives the Marchenko–Pastur law: for purely random returns, every eigenvalue of the correlation matrix must fall inside a known band. Whatever escapes the band is real structure.

λ± = 1 + 1/Q ± 2/√Q,  Q = T/N   — Marchenko–Pastur bounds for random correlations
λmax ≫ λ+   — the market mode: one factor moving everything

This family computes a rolling correlation matrix over a multi-asset returns panel — its API differs from every other family: the input is a dataframe with one column per asset, not OHLCV (input_type="prices" converts prices to returns first) — and reads its structure two ways. Inside each window, assets with a missing value or no variation are dropped, and the window reads NaN if fewer than three usable assets remain. The spectral indicators work on eigenvalues: random matrix deviation measures how far the spectrum escapes the Marchenko–Pastur band (how much genuine correlation exists), summing the excursions above the upper edge and below the lower one, and is undefined unless the window has more rows than assets; market mode strength isolates the largest eigenvalue — the single collective factor that, in crisis, swallows all others — divided by the asset count by default; eigenvalue dispersion summarises how unevenly the whole spectrum is spread, as the standard deviation of all the eigenvalues over their mean. The graph indicators read the matrix as a network: correlation network density is the share of asset pairs whose absolute correlation reaches a threshold (0.5 by default), market connectivity their average absolute coupling, centrality pressure how concentrated the linkage is in a few hub assets — a Herfindahl index of each asset's summed absolute correlations.

Correlation regime shift watches for sudden reorganisations of the whole structure: the normalised Frobenius distance between the correlation matrix of the last 50 rows and that of the full 200-row window. On top sit two composite stress readings, each an average of bounded components: systemic coupling (density, mean absolute correlation, rescaled degree concentration) and network fragility (Marchenko–Pastur excursion, rescaled degree concentration, and a short-versus-long correlation shift over an internal half window).

The physics of interest is the crisis phenomenology: in calm markets correlations are low and the eigenvalue spectrum is mostly noise; under stress, correlations converge toward one, the market mode inflates, and diversification quietly disappears.

When to reach for this family: systemic risk measurement — how coupled the cross-section is, whether that coupling is concentrating, and whether the correlation structure is reorganising.

centrality_pressure

from market_physics.networks import centrality_pressure

centrality_pressure(
    data: pd.DataFrame,
    window: int = 100,
    *,
    input_type: Literal['returns', 'prices'] = 'returns',
    return_method: Literal['pct', 'log'] = 'log',
    min_assets: int = 3,
    normalize: bool = True,
) -> IndicatorResult

This indicator reports how concentrated the cross-asset connectivity is on a few assets. Each asset's weighted degree is the sum of its absolute correlations to the others; the normalised version reports the Herfindahl-style concentration (HHI) of those degrees, while the unnormalised version reports the single largest weighted degree.

The indicator is a descriptive proxy only: it is a centrality-concentration proxy, not a full graph-theoretic centrality and not where any asset will go next.

core quantity sum((degree_i / sum(degree)) ** 2)

Parameters
nametypedefaultdescription
datapd.DataFrame—Multi-asset dataframe (one column per asset).
windowint100Lookback window (rows). Must be at least 3.
input_type kw-onlyLiteral['returns', 'prices']'returns'"returns" uses values directly; "prices" computes column-wise returns first.
return_method kw-onlyLiteral['pct', 'log']'log'How to compute returns when input_type="prices".
min_assets kw-onlyint3Minimum usable assets per window; fewer yields NaN. At least 2.
normalize kw-onlyboolTrueIf True, return the degree-concentration HHI; otherwise the maximum weighted degree.
Returns

An IndicatorResult aligned to data index, with NaN during the warm-up period and wherever a window has fewer than min_assets usable assets. When normalised the value lies in [1 / n_assets, 1].

Raises
ValueErrorIf window is less than 3, input_type / return_method is invalid, min_assets is less than 2, or data has fewer than min_assets columns.
TypeErrorIf data is not a numeric DataFrame.

Example
# returns_panel: DataFrame of asset returns, one column per asset
from market_physics.networks import centrality_pressure

result.name                        # "centrality_pressure"
result.metadata["formula"]         # "sum((degree_i / sum(degree)) ** 2)"
result.values.iloc[-1]             # 0.125405 on the synthetic dataset
result.values.first_valid_index()  # 99 — NaN during warm-up

Reading it — Higher values indicate the connectivity is concentrated on fewer assets; lower values indicate it is spread more evenly. Descriptive only.

Limitation — centrality proxy, not full graph-theoretic centrality

network_fragility(

control

Control theory — feedback, set points, stability · 9 indicators

Control theory is the engineering science of keeping a system at a target. A thermostat, a cruise controller, an autopilot — each continuously measures the error between where the system is and where it should be, and the discipline's core questions are about how that error behaves: does the system correct it, overshoot it, oscillate around it, or diverge from it entirely?

e(t) = r − y(t)   — feedback error: set point minus observed output
overshoot   — how far past the set point a correction carries
stability margin   — how much of the motion acts to shrink the error

The market mapping designates a rolling local baseline of the close as the set point — a rolling mean, with a rolling median also available for feedback error itself — and reads price's behaviour around it in control-theory vocabulary, over a 50-bar window by default. Feedback error is the distance from the baseline (normalised, a z-score-style deviation relative to recent volatility). Control response asks the feedback question directly: have returns historically moved against the prior error (baseline-restoring, like a working controller) or with it (baseline-diverging)? It is the negated rolling correlation between the previous bar's error and the next return, in [−1, 1]. Correction strength signs each return by the previous bar's error direction and averages it relative to the mean absolute return, so +1 means every move was corrective and −1 every move divergent; stability margin re-expresses the same balance as the share of recent movement that was corrective, (1 + correction strength) / 2. Damping efficiency asks how much of the error's magnitude has been shrinking bar over bar — the summed decreases in |e| relative to the summed prior |e|; overshoot pressure averages how far price carries past the baseline after each crossing — the classic step-response overshoot of an under-damped system — relative to the average error size.

The composite readings summarise the loop. Feedback loop intensity blends error size, correction strength and how often the baseline is crossed; the instability score blends amplifying movement, overshoot and weak damping — whether the market currently behaves like a tight, well-damped loop hugging its baseline or an unstable one amplifying its own error; adaptive control pressure pairs the close's distance from a 50-bar baseline with how far that baseline has drifted from a 100-bar reference.

An honest note the module itself insists on: these are control-theory-inspired descriptive features, not a control system — there is no PID logic, no control action, and no claim that a controller governs prices. The family also overlaps knowingly with its neighbours: at matched parameters the normalised feedback error equals stochastic.mean_reversion_pressure on the price, re-interpreted through the set-point lens.

When to reach for this family: mean-reversion quality diagnosis — not just whether price reverts to its local baseline, but how well: promptly and damped, or late, overshooting, and increasingly unstable.

adaptive_control_pressure

from market_physics.control import adaptive_control_pressure

adaptive_control_pressure(
    df: pd.DataFrame,
    window: int = 50,
    *,
    baseline_window: int = 100,
    normalize: bool = True,
    min_valid_components: int = 2,
) -> IndicatorResult

Blends two bounded close-only readings into a single adaptive-baseline-style pressure score: how much the short baseline has drifted away from a longer reference baseline (baseline shift), and how far the close sits from its short baseline (active error). Each is bounded and the score is the mean of the defined components.

"Adaptive" here means the reference baseline changes over time — it is not adaptive trading control. This is a descriptive control-theory-inspired feature, not a control system implementation: it uses no PID controller logic, no automated control loops, and no control action, and it produces no trading signal.

With normalize=False, the raw price-scale components are bounded directly, so values depend on the asset price scale and can saturate for high-priced series; use normalize=True for scale-free readings.

Parameters
nametypedefaultdescription
dfpd.DataFrame—OHLCV dataframe with a close column.
windowint50Short-baseline window. Must be at least 3.
baseline_window kw-onlyint100Long reference-baseline window. Must exceed window.
normalize kw-onlyboolTrueIf True, scale each raw component by the matching rolling standard deviation before bounding.
min_valid_components kw-onlyint2Minimum finite components required to score a bar. Between 1 and 2.
Returns

An IndicatorResult aligned to df index, with values in approximately [0, 1], NaN during the warm-up period and wherever fewer than min_valid_components components are defined.

Raises
ValueErrorIf window is less than 3, baseline_window is not greater than window, or min_valid_components is not between 1 and 2.
MissingColumnErrorIf close is missing.
InsufficientDataErrorIf df has fewer rows than needed for one defined value.
Example
# df: OHLCV dataframe (open, high, low, close, volume)
from market_physics.control import adaptive_control_pressure

result = adaptive_control_pressure(df)
result.name                        # "adaptive_control_pressure"
result.values.iloc[-1]             # 0.36815 on the synthetic dataset
result.values.first_valid_index()  # 99 — NaN during warm-up

Reading it — Higher values indicate stronger adaptive-baseline pressure (a larger short-vs-long baseline shift and a larger deviation of the close from its short baseline); lower values indicate weaker pressure. Descriptive only.

Warm-up note — Composite components may become valid at different times; rows require at least min_valid_components valid components.

Limitation — adaptive means changing baseline/reference behavior, not adaptive trading control. With normalize=False, raw price-scale components are bounded directly, so values depend on the asset price scale and can saturate for high-priced series; use normalize=True for scale-free readings.

geometry

Differential geometry — curvature, geodesics, time dilation · 9 indicators

Differential geometry studies curves and spaces by their intrinsic shape. A curve has a curvature — how sharply it bends at each point; a space has a metric — the rule for measuring distance within it; and the straightest possible path through a space is a geodesic. General relativity made this the deepest language in physics: matter curves spacetime, freely falling bodies follow geodesics, and clocks under stress run at different rates. The geometry family borrows this vocabulary to describe the shape of the price path itself.

κ = |x″| / (1 + x′²)3/2, x = log P   — curvature: how sharply the path bends
L / |Δx|   — path length over net displacement: tortuosity of the route
dτ = dt · f(σ)   — "market time" runs faster in high-volatility stretches

The shape readings are honest plane geometry on the discrete price curve. Price curvature is the second-difference bending of the path — near zero along a straight trend, spiking at V-shaped reversals — computed on log price so that a rescaling of the price drops out, and by default expressed relative to its own 50-bar mean. Trajectory bending sums how much the return changes from bar to bar relative to the summed absolute returns — how much the path zig-zags for the distance it covers. Geodesic deviation compares the distance price actually travelled (arc length) with the straight-line displacement it achieved: the gap is wasted motion, the fraction of the journey spent wandering off the direct route. Path efficiency is the same comparison expressed as a ratio — 1 for a perfectly direct path, falling toward 0 for pure churn; it equals one minus fractals.roughness_index run with a window one bar longer.

The relativistic metaphors extend the language: volatility time dilation treats rolling volatility as the rate at which "market time" passes — stressed markets live through more events per bar — by default relative to its own recent mean; metric distortion asks how stretched the local distance measure is: the current absolute return in units of recent volatility (or, with method="range", the bar's range against its recent mean range), normalised by its own rolling mean; relative motion measures recent drift against a longer reference frame — the 50-bar mean return minus the 200-bar mean, in units of the longer window's volatility. Two composites average bounded versions of these readings: curvature pressure (curvature, bending, metric distortion) and geometry stress (time dilation, metric distortion, geodesic deviation, relative-motion magnitude — curvature deliberately left out so that the two composites do not duplicate each other).

The module is unusually explicit about its epistemics, and the docstrings repeat it: these are geometry-inspired descriptive features. No actual relativity or spacetime model is claimed — and some raw modes coincide with simpler cousins (raw volatility_time_dilation equals stochastic.brownian_volatility at matched parameters; the geometric interpretation is the added value).

When to reach for this family: path-quality measurement — whether recent price action is a clean, efficient, gently-curving route or a tortuous, sharply-bending, stressed one, independent of its direction.

experimental

Measurement metaphors — uncertainty, superposition, resonance · 9 indicators

Every other family in this library transplants an established physical formalism. This one is different, and says so in its name: it borrows measurement metaphors — mostly from the vocabulary of quantum mechanics and resonance physics — and applies them to ordinary rolling return and volume statistics. The metaphors organise intuition; the mathematics underneath is deliberately plain.

uncertainty bandwidth   — rolling volatility read as a measurement's error band
superposition score   — how mixed the up/down "state" of the window is
resonance proxy   — spectral power concentration around a fixed reference period

The measurement metaphors: uncertainty bandwidth reports rolling return volatility as the width of an uncertainty band around the price reading — by default relative to its own recent mean; observer sensitivity asks how much a reading changes when the measurement window itself changes — by default the gap between 20-bar and 50-bar volatility, relative to the 50-bar value, so a large reading means the measurement depends heavily on the window used to take it. The state metaphors: state superposition scores how ambiguous the recent directional state is — a window whose up-bar and down-bar participation (volume-weighted by default) balances is "maximally mixed", a one-sided window has collapsed to a definite state; the transition probability proxy estimates, from recent history, how often the market has hopped between those states — the rolling frequency of sign changes in the return, optionally with a neutral band. The resonance metaphors run a local FFT over 128-bar windows: the fixed-cycle resonance proxy measures how concentrated the return spectrum is around a chosen reference period (20 bars by default), cycle locking how often the window's dominant period stays within 15% of it, and resonance deviation how far the dominant period sits from it. The composite pressure score averages bandwidth, superposition and transition frequency; the regime score adds observer sensitivity and the fixed-cycle reading.

The docstrings are unusually insistent, and the documentation should be too: these are experimental metaphorical proxies only. There is no physical quantum model, no Schumann or Earth-frequency interpretation (reference periods are bars, not Hz), and some indicators coincide with plainer cousins at matched parameters (on data without exactly flat bars, state superposition equals 1 − |microstructure.order_flow_pressure|). Treat the family as a sandbox: name-brand intuitions, commodity statistics, explicitly provisional.

When to reach for this family: exploratory feature generation — ambiguity, measurement-stability, and fixed-cycle readings that complement the established families, clearly labelled as experimental.

cycle_locking_scoreexperimental_pressureexperimental_regime_scorefixed_cycle_resonance_proxyobserver_sensitivityresonance_deviationstate_superposition_scoretransition_probability_proxyuncertainty_bandwidth

cycle_locking_score

from market_physics.experimental import cycle_locking_score

cycle_locking_score(
    df: pd.DataFrame,
    window: int = 128,
    *,
    reference_period: float = 20.0,
    tolerance: float = 0.15,
    return_method: Literal['pct', 'log'] = 'log',
    smoothing_window: int | None = None,
) -> IndicatorResult

Borrowing the metaphor of cycle locking, this indicator measures how often the rolling dominant cycle period stays within a tolerance band around a reference period, smoothed over a short window.

This is an experimental metaphorical proxy only: no physical quantum, Schumann, or resonance model is involved, and it produces no trading signal.

core quantity rolling_mean(locking_event, smoothing_window); locking_event = 1 if abs(dominant_period - reference_period) / reference_period <= tolerance else 0

Parameters
nametypedefaultdescription
dfpd.DataFrame—OHLCV dataframe with a close column.
windowint128FFT window length in bars. Must be at least 8.
reference_period kw-onlyfloat20.0Reference cycle period in bars (positive, resolvable).
tolerance kw-onlyfloat0.15Non-negative relative tolerance band around the reference.
return_method kw-onlyLiteral['pct', 'log']'log'How to compute returns. "pct" uses percentage change; "log" uses log returns.
smoothing_window kw-onlyint | NoneNoneRolling-mean window over the locking events; defaults to max(2, window // 4) when None. Must be at least 1.
Returns

An IndicatorResult aligned to df index, with values in [0, 1], NaN during the warm-up period and for flat/unusable windows.

Raises
ValueErrorIf window is less than 8, reference_period is not positive/resolvable, tolerance is negative, return_method is invalid, or smoothing_window is less than 1.
MissingColumnErrorIf close is missing.
InsufficientDataErrorIf df has fewer than window + smoothing_window rows.
Example
# df: OHLCV dataframe (open, high, low, close, volume)
from market_physics.experimental import cycle_locking_score

result = cycle_locking_score(df)
result.name                        # "cycle_locking_score"
result.metadata["formula"]         # "rolling_mean(locking_event, smoothing_window); locking_event = 1 if abs(dominant_period - reference_period) / reference_period <= tolera..."
result.values.iloc[-1]             # 0 on the synthetic dataset
result.values.first_valid_index()  # 159 — NaN during warm-up

Reading it — Higher values indicate the dominant cycle stayed near the reference period more often within the smoothing window; lower values indicate it did not. Descriptive only.

Related — Thresholded and smoothed dominant-cycle-distance feature. Shares the same local dominant-cycle reference-distance component with resonance_deviation; fixed_cycle_resonance_proxy shares only the local FFT spectrum core and uses the bin nearest the reference period instead of the dominant cycle.

Limitation — Descriptive smoothed cycle-locking condition; not proof of resonance and not predictive. Experimental metaphorical proxy; not a physical quantum, Schumann, or resonance model, and not a trading signal.

microstructure

Agent-based models — order flow, liquidity, impact · 9 indicators

Where most econophysics treats the market as a field or a fluid, agent-based modelling treats it as a many-particle system with intentions: heterogeneous agents submit orders, liquidity providers absorb them, and price emerges from the collision. Market microstructure is the empirical science of that collision — order flow, bid–ask spreads, depth, and the price impact of trading. Its landmark quantities are things like Kyle's lambda (how much price moves per unit of order flow) and the effective spread (the true cost of transacting).

Δp = λ · q   — Kyle: price impact proportional to signed order flow
OFI = Σ sign(move) · participation   — order-flow imbalance over a window
absorption   — heavy participation, muted movement: flow being soaked up

The honest constraint this family imposes on itself — and repeats in every docstring — is that it works from OHLCV bars alone. There is no order book, no bid/ask, no tick data, and no agent simulation; every indicator is a bar-level proxy for a quantity that properly lives at tick resolution. Order flow pressure and volume imbalance sign each bar's volume by its direction and ask which side has been leaning on the tape — the first weights each bar by its volume relative to the 50-bar mean and takes direction from the return, the second uses raw volume and the candle's close versus open. Market impact proxy is bar-level Kyle: movement per unit of participation — high when price glides on thin volume, low when it grinds against heavy flow. Its mirror image is the absorption score: heavy participation that produces little movement means someone is absorbing the flow. Spread proxy reads intrabar range and wicks as transaction friction; liquidity pressure multiplies that relative range by volume participation, so wide bars on heavy volume score high and quiet narrow bars low, and liquidity fragility averages bounded spread, impact and liquidity-pressure readings. The composites — agent pressure (the word is figurative, the module notes; it blends the two imbalance readings with impact) and microstructure stress (five components, in which absorption and impact are inversely related by construction and may partly offset) — blend the bounded readings into single scores.

When to reach for this family: liquidity-regime diagnosis from plain OHLCV — who is leaning on the market, whether flow is being absorbed or is moving price, and how fragile the liquidity underneath appears.

absorption_scoreagent_pressure_scoreliquidity_fragilityliquidity_pressuremarket_impact_proxymicrostructure_stressorder_flow_pressurespread_proxyvolume_imbalance

from market_physics.microstructure import absorption_score

absorption_score(
    df: pd.DataFrame,
    window: int = 50,
    *,
    return_method: Literal['pct', 'log'] = 'log',
    normalize: bool = True,
) -> IndicatorResult

Comparing how much volume participated against how much price actually moved gives an absorption-style reading: heavy participation with muted movement (volume being "absorbed") scores high, while light participation or large movement scores low.

This is a descriptive OHLCV-only microstructure proxy: it is not order-book absorption and it is not an accumulation/distribution signal. It uses no order book, bid/ask, or tick-level trade data.

core quantity raw_absorption = volume_participation / (1 + movement_scale) then / rolling_mean(raw_absorption); volume_participation = volume / rolling_mean(volume), movement_scale = abs(returns) / rolling_mean(abs(returns))

normalize kw-onlyboolTrueIf True, divide the raw absorption by its rolling mean.
Returns

An IndicatorResult aligned to df index, with NaN during the warm-up period and wherever the estimate is undefined (e.g. a zero rolling volume mean or a zero rolling baseline).

Raises

result.name                        # "absorption_score"

result.values.iloc[-1]             # 0.943382 on the synthetic dataset
result.values.first_valid_index()  # 99 — NaN during warm-up

Reading it — Higher values indicate high volume with relatively muted movement (absorption-like behaviour); lower values indicate less absorption-like behaviour. Descriptive only.

Limitation — OHLCV-only microstructure proxy; does not use order book, bid/ask, or tick-level trade data. This is not order-book absorption and not an accumulation/distribution signal.

Example
# df: OHLCV dataframe (open, high, low, close, volume)
from market_physics.microstructure import volume_imbalance

result = volume_imbalance(df)
result.name                        # "volume_imbalance"
result.metadata["formula"]         # "rolling_sum(direction * volume) / rolling_sum(volume), clipped to [-1, 1]; direction = sign(close - open)"
result.values.iloc[-1]             # 0.0423128 on the synthetic dataset
result.values.first_valid_index()  # 49 — NaN during warm-up

Reading it — Positive values indicate volume concentrated in upward candles; negative values indicate volume concentrated in downward candles; values near zero indicate a balanced proxy. Descriptive only.

Related — Closely related to order_flow_pressure at matched direction semantics; volume_imbalance uses raw signed volume, while order_flow_pressure uses normalized volume participation and can be highly correlated.

Limitation — OHLCV-only microstructure proxy; does not use order book, bid/ask, or tick-level trade data. It does not classify trades as buyer- or seller-initiated.

energy

Kinetic energy — mass, velocity, ½mv² · 1 indicator

In classical mechanics a moving body carries kinetic energy E = ½·m·v²: the work it would take to bring it to rest. Two features of that formula matter here. Mass enters linearly, so a heavier body at the same speed carries proportionally more energy; velocity enters squared, so energy has no direction — a body moving one way and a body moving the other way at the same speed are indistinguishable by their energy alone.

v → close-to-close return   — percentage change by default, or log returns
m → volume / rolling_mean(volume, window)   — volume relative to its own recent norm, window = 20 by default
E = ½ · m · v² · scale   — scale only rescales the output for display

The module holds a single function, momentum energy, and it makes the same mapping as the dynamics family: price is position, the bar's return is velocity, and volume relative to its own recent mean is the mass. Because the return is squared, an up move and a down move of the same size on the same volume produce identical energy; High values need a large move, above-average participation, or both; low values a small move, thin volume, or both. The product does not separate the two. It is a per-bar quantity rather than a rolling aggregate — the window only sets the volume baseline, so the first value appears once that baseline exists (index window − 1), and a bar whose rolling volume mean is zero reads NaN.

Its closest relative is dynamics.market_momentum, the signed p = m·v built from the same mass and velocity; that function's docstring draws the distinction explicitly — momentum is signed, momentum energy is not. At matched window and return method, with scale = 1 on both, momentum energy is half of market momentum times the return, E = ½·p·v (equal up to floating-point rounding). dynamics.impulse_energy builds its mass the same way, over its own window (50 bars by default), but measures the move differently — the absolute return in units of its rolling standard deviation over that window, not squared — so it reads how unusual a move is for its recent volatility rather than its raw size. thermodynamics.free_energy_proxy builds its internal-energy term from the same ingredients (a rolling mean of volume-weighted squared returns) but computes it locally rather than calling this function.

When to reach for this family: a direction-free, per-bar measure of how much volume-backed motion a bar carried — the size of a move weighted by its participation, without its sign.

momentum_energy

momentum_energy

from market_physics.energy import momentum_energy

momentum_energy(
    df: pd.DataFrame,
    window: int = 20,
    *,
    return_method: Literal['pct', 'log'] = 'pct',
    scale: float = 1.0,
) -> IndicatorResult

Momentum Energy is inspired by kinetic energy in classical mechanics:

E = 0.5 * m * v^2

Market interpretation:

  • v (velocity) -> close-price return (percentage or log),
  • m (mass) -> normalised volume (current volume relative to its rolling mean),
  • E (energy) -> 0.5 * normalized_volume * return**2.

This indicator measures the energy of movement, not its direction. Because returns are squared, an up move and a down move of the same magnitude produce identical energy. High values indicate strong price moves backed by above-average volume; low values indicate quiet, low-participation moves.

The scale parameter only rescales the output for display/readability (e.g. plotting) and does not change the underlying logic or the relative shape of the series.

core quantity 0.5 * normalized_volume * returns^2

Parameters
nametypedefaultdescription
dfpd.DataFrame—OHLCV dataframe. Requires the close and volume columns.
windowint20Lookback window for the rolling volume mean used to normalise volume (the "mass" term).
return_method kw-onlyLiteral['pct', 'log']'pct'How to compute returns ("velocity"). "pct" uses percentage change; "log" uses log returns.
scale kw-onlyfloat1.0Positive multiplier applied to the final series for easier visualisation. Does not alter the relative shape of the values.
Returns

An IndicatorResult whose values series is aligned to df index, with NaN during the warm-up period and wherever the result is undefined (e.g. zero rolling volume mean).

Raises
ValueErrorIf window is less than 2 or scale is not greater than 0.
MissingColumnErrorIf close or volume is missing.
InsufficientDataErrorIf df has fewer than window rows.
Example
# df: OHLCV dataframe (open, high, low, close, volume)
from market_physics.energy import momentum_energy

result = momentum_energy(df)
result.name                        # "momentum_energy"
result.metadata["formula"]         # "0.5 * normalized_volume * returns^2"
result.values.iloc[-1]             # 1.80324e-05 on the synthetic dataset
result.values.first_valid_index()  # 19 — NaN during warm-up

Reading it — higher means a stronger price move backed by above-average volume, lower means quiet, low-participation movement; direction-free because returns are squared

Limitation — Kinetic-energy analogy on squared returns and normalised volume; not physical energy, not a trading signal, and not predictive. Zero rolling volume mean yields NaN.

core & exceptions

Shared plumbing — result type, validators, exception hierarchy · 10 names

Every family in the library rests on the same small layer. market_physics.core defines the return type and the input checks, and market_physics.exceptions defines the errors those checks raise. Nothing here computes a feature: this is the contract the features share, and the part a caller programs against — or anyone adding an indicator in the same style. IndicatorResult is a slotted dataclass with three fields: name (a string), values (a pd.Series) and metadata (a dict, empty by default). Its constructor checks only those three types and raises TypeError otherwise; the alignment promise — values indexed like the input frame, NaN during warm-up — is kept by each indicator, not enforced by the class. The fields stay assignable after construction (the dataclass is not frozen), but the slots mean no new attribute can be attached. The one public indicator that returns something else is gravity.gravity_levels, a DataFrame of levels.

The validators check only what an indicator actually reads. validate_columns raises TypeError when its input is not a DataFrame and MissingColumnError naming every absent column; because each indicator passes only the columns it uses, OHLCV_COLUMNS (open, high, low, close, volume) is a reference tuple for callers rather than a schema anything enforces. validate_min_rows raises InsufficientDataError when the frame is shorter than a minimum the calling indicator computes itself — typically the rows needed for one defined output, so the minimum differs from function to function. validate_bins is the shared histogram contract used by the entropy, statistical and thermodynamics indicators that build histograms: a BinsSpec is an integer count of at least 2 or one of SUPPORTED_STRING_BINS ("fd", "sqrt", "sturges", forwarded to numpy's histogram). Booleans are refused explicitly, and because the check is isinstance(bins, int), so are floats and numpy integer types such as np.int64(10); all refusals are ValueError.

  • MarketPhysicsError — the base class, a plain Exception subclass in market_physics.exceptions.
  • MissingColumnError — raised by validate_columns; carries .missing and .required as lists, and its message names both.
  • InsufficientDataError — raised by validate_min_rows; carries .available and .required row counts.
  • ValueError / TypeError — parameter errors (a window too small, an unknown mode string, a bad bins) are plain ValueError, and a non-DataFrame input is TypeError; neither subclasses MarketPhysicsError, so catching the base class catches the two data-shape errors only. The networks family checks its wide input with its own helpers (TypeError for a non-DataFrame, ValueError for non-numeric columns or too few assets).

The package top level re-exports IndicatorResult, validate_columns and the three exception classes; validate_min_rows, validate_bins, BinsSpec and the two constants are imported from market_physics.core.

When to reach for this family: writing code around the indicators — catching their data errors, checking a frame before a batch run, or adding an indicator of your own that returns the same contract.
